properties.PropertyDescription: A two storey brick former retail and residential building with a pair of shops. Designed by Inskip & Robertson in the Gothic Revival style. Built for William Henry Welch of the drapers and department stores in 1889. Noted for the four rooftop grotesque kangaroo chimeras and Venetian style windows. The original occupiers were, in the shop, Mr Welch's business Ball and Welch Drapers and on the first floor, the Carlton Club an organisation formed by some affluent local businessmen and politicians of that time. The building has been utilised for a variety of uses. From 1919 until the mid 1920's it was the Yoralla School for Stricken Children. In the 1930's it became known as Herzl Hall and became the meeting place for the Australian Zionist Association of Australia. It has since been refurbished and converted to a restaurant.VHR CitationThe building at 313-315 Drummond Street, Carlton was built in 1889 for Henry William Welch as a two storey commercial premises consisting of two shops with residences. The architects were Inskip and Robertson. The premises were immediately let to the recently formed Carlton Club under the presidency of J Gardiner, MLA for Carlton. The construction is brick with cement dressings on a basalt plinth. The main facade is symmetrical and dominated by a ground floor replica cast iron verandah and by the Gothic styling of the upper storey. Four pairs of round arched windows with polychromatic brick arches are divided by piers with a band of pressed cement decorative foliation at their base. The arches are framed by pointed arch drip moulds linked by gargoyle spouts. Beneath each window is a cement panel incorporating a decorative foliation pattern. Three cement roundels, each with a high-relief mask of a king's head, sit in the spandrels between each pair of drip moulds. The cornice is bracketed. The parapet is divided by four piers, each with a grotesque on top. The identical and cleanly modelled grotesques are hybrids of a kangaroo and gryphon, each with three toes, a tail and carrying a shield. The central section of the parapet is slightly raised with plain pilaster decoration. The flanking sections of the parapet have a repeating trefoil motif. Despite being linked internally, the ground floor facade can be read as two shop fronts divided by pilasters. The two large panes of glass to each of the fronts are divided by a recessed doorway. Iron supports around each entrance are evidence of a previous shutter system. Above the main glazing is a frieze of pointed arches with leaded glass. At the rear is a Johns & Co cast iron spiral fire escape staircase of unknown date.The building at 313-315 Drummond Street, Carlton is architecturally significant for its highly unusual grotesque Gothic facade. Contributing to this effect are the cornice and the parapet incorporating Gothic motifs, the chimera, the roundels incorporating high-relief masks and the original shopfront with a frieze of leaded glass Gothic windows over the main panes and matching Gothic style doors. The styling of the facade is reminiscent of the horizontal Gothic of Venice and deliberately alludes to the commercial prestige of that city. The kangaroo-gryphon grotesques on the parapet are highly unusual and distinctive. The proto-nationalist symbol, the kangaroo, has been medievalised. The grotesques anticipate a later general patriotic preference for the use of native animals as roofline decoration.The building at 313-315 Drummond Street, Carlton is historically significant for its associations with the Carlton Club, the first occupiers of the building. The establishment of the Carlton Club is significant as an expression of middle class affluence and business success in the Carlton area in the late 1880s.

properties.PropertyDescription:
A consolidation of three seperate properties now owned by the University of Melbourne and used as a hall of residence known as Medley Hall.

At 46 Drummond is a two storey rendered brick residence. Known as Rosaville it was built for Abraham Harris the importer and retailer in 1883. Designed by Nahum Barnet in the Free Classical style it is a good example of Melbourne's boom style classicism of the 1880's.

At 48-54 Drummond is a two storey rendered brick townhouse known as Benvenuta. Designed by Walter Scott Law in the Free Classical style it was built for Mrs Leah Abrahams by Richard Stockdale in 1893. Of note is the central tower, two tiered arcade and elaborate stuccowork and mouldings. It is thought to be Mr Law's finest work.
In 1925 the Commonwealth Government leased the property and refurbished it converting it into Arbitration Court Offices. In the early 1930's it was converted to an Italian Social Club and it housed the Italian Consulate until the beginning of WW2. The University took over and utilised it as a hostel in 1953. 
In 1955 it became Medley Hall.

At 56 Drummond is a two storey rendered brick townhouse. Built for Mr Joseph Levy in 1886. When these properties were purchased by the University a rear extension of four storeys was added.

properties.PropertyDescription: A rendered brick building of two and three storeys. Formerly known as Frosterley after the village in Durham from where the builder of the property, John Snowball, originated. Built for his son the paediatrician Dr William Snowball as a medical surgery and residence in 1890. At the time Dr Snowball was the Chairman of the medical staff at the Children's Hospital. After Dr Snowball's death in 1902 the building was leased to University High School as a residence for country boarders. In 1908 the property was purchased by the Commonwealth Government. It was refurbished and it became the Headquarters of the newly formed Commonwealth Bureau of Meteorology. In 1939 the three storey annex facing Victoria Street was completed. It remained as the headquarters for the Bureau untl 1974 when it was then utilised by the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology. In 1999 it was sold then refurbished, subdivided and converted to nine residential units.

properties.PropertyDescription:
A religious complex featuring a Church and a two storey hall and presbytery.

It was decided to create two parishes from the West Melbourne Parish and in 1901 the site was purchased for 1,700 pounds. In April 1903 the new parish of North Melbourne was declared and the Reverend John Norris was appointed parish priest.
The first building erected was the hall and presbytery. Built at a cost of 550 pounds it is a red brick building of two storeys with a terracotta tiled roof. Of an early Edwardian styling it features a simple Romanesque three arched entrance arcade with the equivalent first storey landing. It was opened on Sunday 6th September 1903 by Archbishop Thomas Carr. Archbishop Carr used his speech to express his dismay at what he perceived was a growing sectarian intolerance that was permeating society. As reported by the Argus Newspaper of 7th September 1903 Archbishop Carr said There existed in their midst an organisation, whose avowed objects were to exclude Catholics from the legislature of the country, and from municipal life, and, without doubt, a part of its action, if not of its policy, was to exclude Catholics from all position of emolument. Further referring to the vexed question of religious instruction in state schools he said If adequate religious instruction was to be given, it must be given separately to children of the different religious persuasions. Any mixed system, if it were not injurious to some, be imperfect for all. Mr Henry Higgins the M.H.R. for North Melbourne in reply to the Archbishop's speech said that he always opposed forcing on the state schools any system of religious training. All denominations stood upon a level in these matters, and it was not right to force the Protestant scriptures on the state schools. He was himself a Protestant, but had always voted against any such proposal when in the Victorian Parliament. This was met with cheers.

The foundation stone for the Church was laid by Archbishop Carr on Sunday 9th June 1907 and the building was completed in early 1908. It was designed by the firm Grainger Kennedy & Little who had designed the Northern Administration Annexe of the Melbourne Town Hall. Mr John Grainger, a principal of the firm, was the father of the famed composer Percy Grainger. Designed in the Edwardian style with Romanesque features it is built of red brick with limestone dressings and has a slate roof. The interior features paintings by the itinerant Italian artist Giorgio de Pyro. The cost of construction and furnishing the building was 8,000 pounds. When the debt of this was dealt with, the Church was consecrated by the Most Reverend John McCarthy, Bishop of Sandhurst on Thursday 29th October 1925. The Reverend Norris was still in charge of the parish and remained so until his death in 1941 at the age of eighty.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: A municipal complex of a townhall and ancillary buildings. The former Borough of Kensington and Flemington Town Hall is a two storey brick public building. It features a stuccoed facade of highly decorated classical features and a brick mansard tower. Designed by Evander McIver and built by Mr W F Holden in 1901 for a cost of around £6,000. It included municipal offices, a council chamber, a library and a public hall capable of seating 600 persons. The site was chosen by a referendum of the ratepayers. The foundation stone was laid by the Mayoress Mrs C J Davies and the Mayor, Councillor J P Davies on Thursday 14th March 1901. In May 1905, after a poll of ratepayers voted for unification, the Borough and the Town of North Melbourne were annexed and amalgamated  with the City of Melbourne. The former borough became the new Council Ward of Hopetoun and on December 1st the first election for Councillors was held. During World War 2 a secret underground army communication control centre was accessed through a trapdoor under the stage of the public hall. Other buildings include the Child Welfare Centre at 22 Bellair Street that was built in 1935 and two other single storey brick buildings built in the 1960's. In 2014 the townhall building was refurbished for a cost of $3.5m.

A steel clocktower built in 1939 is situated in the courtyard.

The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: Built on the site of the Polytechnic Hall which housed the Theatre Comique later renamed the Hall of Science. A six storey brick building with a stuccoed facade. Originally of four storeys when first built it had four ground level shops. A fine example of Late Melbourne Boom Style architecture. It was designed by Billing & Son in conjunction with Oakden Addison & Kemp. It is described as designed in the Elizabethan Revival style with noted French Second Empire flourishes. It was built for the Young Christian Men's Association by Mr H Maxwell. The cost of land and construction was £55,000. Finance for the project came from £20,000 for the sale of real estate, a £20,000 mortgage and £10,000 from promised subscriptions. There was a shortfall of £5,0000 which the YMCA was confident of gaining from the rental of the shops, the hiring of the facilities and membership payments. The foundation stone was laid by Governor Lord Hopetoun on Tuesday 22nd April 1890 and it was opened by the Justice Minister, Mr John Mark Davies, on 27th January 1891. A grand affair, attendees included politicians and leaders of the various protestant churches. The Anglican clergy sent their apologies as they were attending ceremonies associated with opening of the new cathedral. A bright future was predicted for the building and organisation. Unfortunately, the great financial catastrophe which began in 1892 put paid to this. The rentals of the shops had to be lowered, the promised subscriptions were not forthcoming and the mortgage could not be met. In 1894 the property was sold to the Salvation Army for £19,500. In January 1895, after a refurbishment costing £2,000, it became the Salvation Army Headquarters for Australia. The building was dedicated by Commissioner T Coombs on January 24th. In 1897 the attic was converted to Australia's first dedicated film studio. In 1898 the rear of the top floor was incorporated into the studio. Directed by Major Joseph Henry Perry it became the Limelight Department which specialised in cinematgraph and limelight production. It became a maker and producer of many important early films. A notable early success was the production of 'Soldiers of the Cross'. Conceived by Commandant Herbert Booth, the son of the Army's founder Henry Booth, as a visual compliment to a series of lectures he gave around Australia and New Zealand. It premiered in The Melbourne Town Hall on the 13th September 1900. Said to be Australia's first feature film, it was in fact a series of 200 coloured lantern slides interspersed with fifteen, nine second films with live oratory and music. In effect a multi-media production. It featured the lives of the early Christian martyrs. So florid were the scenes of violence several ladies were said to have fainted in the aisles at the premier. Following the success of this the NSW Government contracted the Limelight Department to record the birth of the Australian Nation at Federation. This became known as 'The Inaugaration of the Australian Commonwealth'. The first documentary made in Australia and running at thirty minutes it was the longest film yet made. In 1909 the production facility was transferred to a new studio in Malvern. In 1910 the new leader, Commissioner Hay, wary of the moral effects of film closed the Limelight Department. In 1953 a lift was installed at a cost of £7,000. Between 2008 and 2011 it was refurbished and redeveloped with the addition of the top two storeys.  A purpose built museum was created that incorporated  the original film studio. The architect for the project was Michael Taylor Architecture and Heritage and the builder was APM Group.

properties.PropertyDescription: A three storey rendered brick arcade including a basement with entrances to Bourke, Little Collins and Elizabeth Streets. Designed for the barrister Howard Spensley by Charles Webb in the Italianate style. It was built in 1869 by Thomas Newton at a contracted price of £14,039. properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The new century brought with it new materials and sustainable projects that depending on your point of view, are astonishing or an eye sore; they are designed to be noticed.
Museums, residential skyscrapers, stadiums and public and University buildings alike have been designed and modelled on computers in 3D and constructed with precision.
No one single style is dominant, with architects experimenting with highly conceptual and expressive styling resembling art and sculpture on a grand scale.

properties.PropertyDescription: A six storey concrete office building with a mezzanine and ground level retail. The facade is constructed with a mix of brick, sandstone and polished granite with some rendered surfaces. Designed in the Modern Romanesque style by Oakley & Parkes and built by Weavell & Keast in 1931. It features an arched arcade entrance and was built on the site of Melbourne's first synagogue.Site is being redeveloped in 2019 to incorporate a Hotel at the rear off Little Queen Street and a Restaurant/Bar.
properties.VHR: Statement of Significance Equity Chambers was constructed in 1930-31 to the designs of the architects Oakley & Parkes, and was built by Weavell & Keast for £90,000. The site was that of the first synagogue in Victoria. Equity Chambers was built for the Equity Trustees Company, which had been established in 1888 by an Act of the Victorian Parliament to provide trustee and executor services, and later evolved into a financial services provider. The building was designed to accommodate the Equity Trustees offices and an impressive main chamber on the ground floor, the company's offices on the first floor and tenants on the upper floors. The building was close to Melbourne's legal quarter and mainly served members of the legal profession. The legal chambers were set up by Sir Eugene Gorman in 1931 and the third floor in particular has had a close association since then with a number of judges and barristers which have been prominent in Victoria's legal history.Equity Chambers is a steel-framed and reinforced concrete office building in an Inter-war Romanesque style, with a basement, ground floor, mezzanine and four upper floors. The front elevation is faced with tapestry brickwork on a double storey plinth of Sydney sandstone and polished granite. The upper windows are recessed with decorated spandrels. The facade is crowned by a terracotta band, the projecting central bay being elaborately decorated with multi-coloured terracotta tiles, corbels supporting pointed arches, and decorated square panels. Stylistically the details are derived from Italian Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The central entrance is through an arcaded porch, with the name 'Equity Trustees Company' inscribed above in Art Deco style lettering. The porch, supported by two polished granite columns, opens into a hallway with a vaulted coffered ceiling leading to the large rear main chamber, which retains decorative plasterwork, Corinthian columns, carved timber surrounds on the door into the entry hall and the staircase to the mezzanine offices. Two lifts are located in a passage which is perpendicular to the central main hall. Notable original features include the incised foliated bands and other facade decoration, the arcaded entry porch, the entrance foyers with their coffered ceilings, the elaborately decorated post box and fire alarm in the lift foyer, the patterned timber veneer lined lift cars and the stairways.This site is part of the traditional land of the Wurundjeri people.Equity Chambers is architecturally significant as an outstanding example of the exotic revival architectural styles which were adopted in Victoria during the inter-war period, especially during the Great Depression. It is significant as a demonstration of the then characteristic application of historically inspired architectural detail to contemporary building forms. The Italian Romanesque and Gothic detailing is particularly fine, and the ground floor loggia, entry foyer and lift interiors are among the finest in Victoria. It was one of the few large buildings constructed in Melbourne during the Great Depression, when economy, as well as appearance, was a prime concern.Equity Chambers is historically significant as the oldest continuously occupied barristers' chambers in Victoria, which have been occupied since 1931 by some of Victoria's most famous judges and barristers.Last updated on - April 19, 2010

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

properties.PropertyDescription: Seven storey rendered concrete department store with basement. The Myer Emporium, mainly constructed in stages during the 1920s and 1930s to designs by the leading commercial architects of the time, HW & FB Tompkins, and built by C Langford are of State significance. Together, the buildings formed a merchandising enterprise that in 1929 was described as one of the largest in the British Empire.The Mural Hall, a dining hall for 1,000 people and a venue for fashion parades and performances, was completed in 1933 as part of the sixth floor which was set aside for dining. It is a large rectangular space with a decorative plaster ceiling and balconies and wall panels in a Streamline Moderne style. At the north end of the hall, a pair of ‘mannequin stairs’ lead down from two balconies and the change rooms to a common landing. A temporary catwalk or stage was installed at this landing level for fashion parades and performances. The Hall is decorated with ten murals by renowned artist Napier Waller (1893–1972). Mural Hall is currently used exclusively as a private event space.Myer was extensively renovated from 2009 to 2011.
properties.VHR: The Myer Emporium is a department store which occupies an extensive area between Bourke and Lonsdale Streets in Melbourne. The Bourke Street store is located at 314-336 Bourke Street and extends through to 297-309 Little Bourke Street and the Lonsdale Street store is located at 275-321 Lonsdale Street and extends through to 280-84 and 290-316 Little Bourke Street. The area includes ten buildings acquired or constructed by Melbourne businessman and philanthropist Sidney Myer between 1911 and 1934. The first building constructed by Myer was the 1914 Bourke Street building. The new parts of the complex were constructed in stages to the designs of leading Melbourne commercial architects HW and FB Tompkins. The laneways bordering the Myer Emporium include Staughton Place, Lynch Place and Arcade Alley and Angelo Lane.The former Robertson & Moffat Buildings, South (1881-84), the western section designed by Crouch & Wilson and the eastern section by William Salway (297-311 Little Bourke Street) and North ( 1890) designed by William Salway, 290-292 Little Bourke Street) , the Former Slatter's Building (1892 ) designed by Nahum Barnet (283 Lonsdale Street) and the Former Clarke's building (1892-93) designed by Nahum Barnet (275-281 Lonsdale Street) were purchased by Myer at different times. Their interiors have been altered extensively but the buildings remain significant in demonstrating the history of retailing in Melbourne, and forming part of the larger significance of the history of the Myer Emporium.The Little Bourke Street Pharmacy, a three story brick building, constructed in c.1910 was purchased by Myer in 1981 and the site of the Little Shop, at 280-84 Little Bourke Street was purchased by Myer in 1951.The facades of the Lonsdale and Little Bourke Street buildings exhibit Classical and Beaux Arts influences while the Bourke Street facade is a notable example of the Interwar Art Deco style finished in 'Snowcrete' (British White Portland Cement), a new product in the 1930s: this has since been painted. The present Bourke Street facade, eight storeys in height, spanning 200 feet (78.74 metres), was completed in 1933 and brought together a section built in 1914 (east) and a section built in 1933 to give the appearance of one building. It takes up the space of what were previously three separate buildings. The Drum Clock, suspended 72 feet (28.34 metres) above the pavement on the Bourke Street facade, is also a significant exterior feature. The sixth floor Mural Hall was also completed at this time.A major change to the ground floor Bourke Street facade was made in 1955, and included new window treatments at ground floor level with black granite surrounds, the addition of cantilever awnings at first floor level on Bourke and Lonsdale Streets. The original lighting and signage were removed at this time. Other changes included the addition of the pedestrian bridge between the Bourke and Lonsdale Street stores over Little Bourke Street in 1962. This linked the Bourke and Lonsdale Street stores at first, second and third floor levels. Illuminated 'Myer' signs (fabricated from aluminium framing and internally illuminated acrylic panels) and clocks are fixed to the western and eastern sides of the pedestrian bridge at first floor level. The upper storey windows of the Bourke and Lonsdale Street facade have been overpainted and many changes have been made to the interiors since the 1930s.The Mural Hall, a dining hall for 1000 people and a venue for fashion parades and performances, was completed in 1933 as part of the sixth floor which was set aside for dining. It is a large rectangular space with a decorative plaster ceiling and balconies and wall panels in a Streamline Moderne style. At the north end of the hall, a pair of "mannequin stairs" lead down from two balconies and the change rooms to a common landing. A temporary catwalk or stage was installed at this landing level for fashion parades and performances. The balustrading of the stairs is formed from 'Staybrite' stainless steel in an abstract ribbon design and the handrail is polished timber. The Hall is decorated with ten murals by renowned artist Napier Waller (1893-1972). The original timber flooring was replaced by parquetry in 1960. The hall is lit by three large and elaborate chandeliers from the original decorative scheme which were designed to provide up to ten different lighting effects.The Lamson pneumatic tube cash conveying system was installed in the store in 1914 with the dispatch station in the basement and cash terminal stations on other floors fed by concealed tubing in the walls. Lamson systems had been invented in the 1880s, and included overhead wire systems for smaller stores and the more sophisticated pneumatic tube system of cash stations and tubes installed inside the walls of large department stores. The system at Myer consists of a series of embossed ornate chambers and chutes, with chrome-plated cast brass, leather valves, push rods and balancing gear. The system is largely intact, though steel tubing which originally connected to the store's various departments, has been cut off at ceiling level in parts. A secondary cash station is still extant in a storage area at the northern end of the fifth floor of the Bourke Street store. This ornate pneumatic tube system is extremely rare and is the only known example of its type to survive in situ in Victoria.Simcha (Sidney) Baevski was born in 1878 in Kritchev, Russia, and migrated to Australia in 1898 to join his elder brother Elcon who was working in the drapery business in Melbourne. In 1901, after adopting the family name of Myer, Sidney and Elcon moved to Bendigo, and established a drapery store in Hargreaves Street. The first Myer store was established in Melbourne in 1911 in the Bourke Street premises of the drapery business, Wright & Neil. Myer expanded the business rapidly, influenced by overseas trends in retailing and a visit to the United States in 1910, and by 1914 was able to construct a new store known as the Myer Emporium to a design by H.W. and F.B. Tompkins. The eight-storey Myer Emporium opened on 5 August 1914 and its frame still exists within the fabric of the present Bourke Street store. The design for a new eleven-storey Lonsdale Street store was by H.W. and F.B. Tompkins and construction began in 1925.Part of the success of the Myer retailing technique was due to the innovative use of sophisticated window displays. Sidney Myer relied on the Myer Bourke Street windows to attract customers, using theatrical sets and model figures to display goods, instead of a conglomeration of miscellaneous goods. New lines were first introduced in the windows. From 1925, a separate department within the store was devoted to display design and installation. New windows were installed to Bourke Street in 1955 and the tradition of the decorated Myer Christmas windows commenced at the time of the Olympic Games in 1956 with windows representing 'Santa Claus and the Olympics'. Each year a different theme is illustrated in the windows with later Christmas windows featuring illustrations of fairy tales. The complex continues to operate as a department store with Myer family involvement.The Myer Mural Hall is aesthetically significant as a rare and intact surviving example of a Streamline Moderne department store dining room. The Myer Mural Hall contains large-scale interior mural works, including representations of women through the ages, by Napier Waller, a leading neo-classical mural painter of the Inter-War period.The Myer Emporium is architecturally significant for its design by prominent Melbourne commercial architects H.W. and F.B. Tompkins.T0001

properties.PropertyDescription: An eight storey brick office building with basement and ground level retail. Formerly a three storey warehouse it was purchased by Mr Norman Sharpe from the clothier Leopold Leber in 1932 for 38,000 pounds. Mr Sharpe, a successful merchant from Morwell who had established a chain of stores in Gippsland, refurbished the building for 5,000 pounds and established a drapery emporium which  he named Norman's Corner Store. In 1935 the building was completely rebuilt with the addition of  five extra storeys at a cost of 15,000 pounds. The reconstruction was designed by Marcus Barlow in the Jazz Moderne style. Subdivided into 23 commercial units in 2003.

It incorporates two shops of the same age at 168 and 170 Bourke Street. It was renamed Stutt's Hotel in the early 1870's, Morell's Family Hotel in the mid 1890's and then Richardson's Hotel in 1907. It was sold to the National Bank of Australasia in 1955 and converted to a bank. In 2009 it was refurbished and converted to shops.

Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription:
Urban Camp is a two storey iron & timber buildings and stands in an area of Royal Park which in 1941 was known as Camp Pell. The Camp was used by American troops stationed in Australia. Troops slept under canvas on army stretchers, cooking facilities were limited and there was no hot water. Camp Pell steadily expanded. Metal huts were added to provide more space. Anzac Hall is a simple and functional building principally of timber and corrugated iron very like recreation halls at other major encampments, its only unusual features being its composite timber and steel rod roof trusses and its sliding and folding door system. There are also some stone sentry boxes, gateposts, stairs and retaining wall nearby.

Anzac Hall was completed in 1941 for the RSL as a cinema, lecture and recreation hall. Soldiers enjoyed sports matches of baseball, cricket and football on the site and the Camp's mascot, Buddy the Galah, was trained to answer the office phone and provided much amusement. In August 1945 the war in the Pacific officially ended. Americans were no longer required for occupation and returned home. Royal Park became a principal demobilisation centre for service personnel and a cheerful disassembly point as troops packed up operations. Camp Pell was decommissioned in December 1945.

After the war, Camp Pell was used by the Housing Commission for emergency public housing. In 1946, 3,000 people were moved into what became known as 'Camp Hell'. This emergency housing was intended to last one year. However, the last inhabitants moved out in 1956 - after ten years of hardship and poverty. Dedicated caretakers ran the Camp from an office in Anzac Hall.

In 1956, the tin huts of Camp Pell were demolished and the site cleaned up. Royal Park was returned to public parkland in time for the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games.

Anzac Hall was left behind after the clearance and the hall remained unused from 1956 - 1970, when Kensington High School teachers gained permission from City of Melbourne to refurbish the Hall for educational use. At this time, some thought Anzac Hall should be demolished.

The Urban Camp Melbourne Co-operative opened in 1984, when teachers from Kensington Community School suggested using Anzac Hall as community camp accommodation for country visitors to the city. Funds were obtained from the Federal Government for the employment of staff and a lease was organised through the City of Melbourne. The Camp provided affordable accommodation in Melbourne for country/rural schools and rural visitors in the late 1980s. In 1986 an inspection found that the buildings needed considerable repair. Fortunately, money for the emergency work was raised and The Camp continued to operate. In 1987, after much discussion, facilities were improved and extended to bring an increase of visitors to the camp. The redevelopment preserved the heritage values of camp buildings and enhanced the natural assets of the surrounding parkland.

In 2000 Anzac Hall was put on the Victorian Heritage Register as significant. Urban Camp went from strength to strength with ongoing government funding and many regular customers, it celebrated its 10th anniversary in 1994.

From 1998 – 2002 extensive rebuilding took place. This included refurbishment of Anzac Hall and the construction of a new North Wing, including a two-storey dormitory section. As the Urban Camp celebrates its 25th anniversary in 2009, it has become extremely popular – often booked years in advance by returning clientele. From difficult beginnings, The Camp now operates as a thriving community-owned enterprise. Urban Camp provides a city camp base for thousands of community groups and young visitors from country Victoria, interstate and overseas each year. Many come to experience and learn about life in the city and enjoy the cultural, sporting and educational assets Melbourne has to offer.

properties.PropertyDescription: Public reserve.

A subway connecting Degraves Street with Flinders Street Station and used as a retail arcade. Named after the driving force behind the project and chairman of the Melbourne City Council's public works committee, Councillor Robert Burns Campbell. Built as part of the modernisation of Melbourne stimulated by the coming of the 1956 Olympics. Work on its construction began late in 1952 and it was opened on July 1st 1955. It was built by the open cut method rather than tunnelling causing. The cost of the project was £400,000. It features late art deco shop fronts. The glass showcases are now used for art installations.

It is a stone cairn located on the departure site of 1860 and erected in 1890.

properties.PropertyDescription: Concrete building.

Known as Tasma Terrace. A row of six, three storey rendered brick terraces designed by Charles Webb.Formerly composed of seven terraces number 14 was demolished in the 1940's. Numbers 8 to 12 were built by William Ireland in 1878 for Mr. George Nipper. Mr. Nipper, a grain merchant and ship owner, later contracted Mr. Webb to design the Grand Hotel (now known as the Windsor) in Spring Street. Numbers 2 to 6 were built by Dunton & Herudon for Mr. Joseph Thompson in 1887. Mr. Thompson was a well known bookmaker and sporting entrepreneur. He was particularly active in the promotion of boxing.The property is managed by the National Trust on behalf of the Victorian State Government.
properties.OriginalOwner: Mr George Nipper, Mr Joseph Thompson
properties.VHR: Tasma terrace, once comprising seven three storey buildings, was constructed in two stages. The first three buildings were erected in 1878-78 by William Ireland for George Nipper, grain merchant and shipowner. The remaining four buildings were constructed in 1886-87 by Dunton and Hearnden for Joseph Thompson, bookmaker. The architect for the completion of the terrace and probably for the earlier stage was Charles Webb. One of the buildings was demolished c.1940, the rear wings were also demolished c.1972Tasma terrace is a rare example of a three storey terrace development despite having one of the dwellings and all of the rear wings demolished the remaining sections are substantially intact.Tasma terrace is an important work of the distinguished architect, Charles Webb, whose other works include Wesley College (1864), Alfred hospital (1869), Royal Arcade (1869) and the Grand hotel, later the Windsor (1884).Tasma Terrace, the subject of a major preservation battle from 1970-72 holds an important place in the history of building conservation in the state of Victoria. The preservation campaign resulted in the government enacting legislation in 1972 which established the government buildings advisory council, Australia's first legislation for the preservation of government owned historic buildings.Tasma terrace demonstrates the entrepreneurial optimism which characterised the boom period of Victoria's history in the late 1870s and 1880s.

properties.PropertyDescription:
The Reserve has 2 important features within and nearby.

The Great Petition artwork was created by artists Susan Hewitt and Penelope Lee and launched on 3rd December 2008 to celebrate the 100 year anniversary of women's right to vote in Victoria. It provides an impressive and enduring focus on the issue of women's contribution to public life and was commissioned by the State Government of Victoria in collaboration with the City of Melbourne. The artwork, fabricated in rolled steel and painted in parchment white, is a contemporary reading of the Monster Petition, a giant petition of 30,000 signatures offered to the Victorian Parliament in 1891 as evidence of widespread support for equal voting rights for women. The continuing opposition of the parliament, which knocked back numerous Bills, meant that women had to wait another seventeen years before they were given voting rights with the passage of the Adult Suffrage Act in 1908.  The petition has been digitised and can be searched online for the names of the signatories.

The other feature of note, is the historic Tram Shelter in the south west corner. This shelter is a VicTrack asset and included on the Victorian Heritage Register (VHR H1870). The tram shelter is of architectural significance as one of only five remaining tram shelters from the city cable tram network which were designed as picturesque pavilions in the domestic Edwardian style of the period.

The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: A two storey brick on a bluestone base former factory with a basement. Designed by Mr Charles Webb, designer of the Windsor Hotel, in the Italianate style and built for the Banks & Co Clothing Company by Mr Henry Lockington of Carlton in 1884. A two storey caretaker's residence was erected to the rear of the factory. The cost of construction and the installation of machinery and fittings was upwards of 8,500 pounds. A hydraulic lift was installed running from the basement to the top storey. It employed up to 225 workers with a weekly wages bill of 250 pounds. In its day it was considered one of the most modern and innovative clothing factories in Victoria with the power for the machinery coming from a 6 1/2 hp Otto gas engine. To quote from the Argus Newspaper of 14 May 1885  The machines employed for white work, for underclothing &c are run at the rate of between 1,400 and 1,500 stitches a minute, but for tweeds and heavy goods about 1,000 stitches is a good average speed .  By the 1970's it had discontinued as a factory and was utilised as a warehouse. In 1991 it was refurbished and converted to offices and ground level retail.

properties.PropertyDescription:
The Melbourne General Cemetery was established in 1853.

As a consequence of the overcrowding and state of disrepair of Melbourne's previous General Cemetery located in West Melbourne (now the site of the Queen Victoria Market) and after much agitation and lobbying from Melbourne interests to the Colonial Legislative Council in NSW the Melbourne General Cemetery Bill was assented by the Governor on 19th September 1850. A budget of 500 pounds was allocated to facilitate the enclosing, fencing and laying out of the new Melbourne Cemetery. The site was selected, Trustees were appointed and in 1852 the surveyor and architect Albert Purchas was contracted to design the layout.
The design, based on the latest European idea of the cemetery as not just a place of internment but of an aesthetically pleasing park, was accepted. The Argus Newspaper of February 7th 1852, who was in whole hearted agreement with this design concept, stated … and the burial place, ceasing to be a dismal and dangerous spot, has become a pleasing retreat for affectionate recollection and pensive meditation. At the time there were two variations of this theme, these being, the Gardenesque and the Picturesque. The Gardenesque a formal design was developed by the Scottish horticulturalist John Claudius Loudon. It featured strong lines and formalised plantings. The Picturesque was first developed in France and then avidly adopted by the Americans and English. It was considered a romantic style being less formal and utilising more natural landscaping elements. Mr Purchas incorporated elements of both styles in his design and these can be seen today with the Picturesque represented by the curving roadways and the Gardenesque by the symmetrical layout of paths, regular siting of burial plots and the use of regular rows of plantings, particularly conifers.

As was the custom of the day, the layout allocated space to the various religious denominations then active in Melbourne. This was based on the census of 1851. This census divided the religious affiliations as Church of England, Church of Scotland, Weslyan Methodists, other Protestants, Roman Catholics, Jews, Mohomedans, Pagans and other persuasions. At the time of this census it was noted that Melbourne's population was 23,143 and the Colony of Victoria totaled 77,345. By the 1854 census it had increased to 47,722 and 236,776 respectively. It should be noted that the aboriginal population was not registered in these census. Victoria's Registrar-General, Major Norman Campbell, in his preface to the census report stated No note appears to have been taken of the aboriginal tribes, with the exception of a very few individuals who were employed on stations …. The estimated number of aborigines (in Victoria) is stated to be about 2,500, but no certain information respecting them has been obtained. In 1859 the land grant was extended to its present size. This was formalised in the Crown Grant of 1871 which named the trustees and assigned the space to the various denominations. The schedule stated (approx.) that the Church of England was to have 29 acres, Roman Catholics to have 17 acres, Presbyterians to have 11 acres, Weslyans to have 5 acres, the Independent Church to have 4 acres, Baptists to have 3 acres, Jews to have 1 acre, Society of Friends to have 1 acre, Lutherans to have 2 roods and 31 perches, Unitarians to have 1 rood and 32 perches and other denominations to have 3 acres. By the 1870's about an acre was reserved for the Chinese population.

The horticultural aspect of the cemetery developed and changed over the years. It was dependent on the current fashion of the day and the requirement for space for the burial plots and monuments. Between 1860 and 1871 the Government Botanist, Ferdinand Von Mueller, supplied and directed the planting of much of the material. Herr von Mueller took the formal approach and his favoured plant materials, reflecting his Northern European origins, were conifers such as cluster pines, Cryptomerias and cypresses. In 1873 Clement Hodgkinson, the surveyor and government administrator, became the Planting Adviser to the Trust. He came with his own ideas preferring the less formal approach and substantially rearranged and replaced much of what Herr von Mueller had created. Mr Hodgkinson died in 1893 and, fittingly, he was buried in the Melbourne General Cemetery. By the 1880's these plantings were matured and the cemetery had become a popular place for the public to visit. They were treated with not only the pleasure of promenading amongst the many trees but the sight of waterfalls, grottos, flower beds and expansive areas of manicured lawns. As space for burials became more imperative much of these early plantings and landscape features have disappeared. Today there is still some evidence of these plantings and the site contains good examples of coast redwood, Canary Island pine, pepper tree and most notably a rare long-leaved Indian pine (Pinus roxburghii) that is registered with the National Trust.

Most of the original structures in the cemetery were wooden. By the 1870's these were being replaced by brick and stone buildings. The oldest building is the Jewish Memorial Chapel built in 1854 and fully restored in 2000. The most substantial building is the Roman Catholic Funeral Chapel. Designed in the Gothic style by William Wardell and built of bluestone in 1871 with the Southern and Northern wings added in 1889. Originally designed over two crypts intended as the final resting place for up to 100 clergymen. On Sunday 10th September, after a procession starting from St Francis's Church, the blessing of the chapel was conducted by the Right Reverend Dr. Goold in front of a crowd estimated at between 10-15,000 persons. The original Gatekeepers Lodge a two storey bluestone building designed by Charles Webb in the Gothic style was built in 1870. It was reconstructed on its present site in the South-Eastern corner in 1935 and has been refurbished and converted to an administrative centre. Of interest are the Chinese Funerary Ovens that were used for the Confucianism rites of the Chinese community. A legacy of Albert Purchas' original design are the cast iron octagonal rotundas scattered throughout the site. The boundary fence was completed by Jageurs & Son in 1876.

It is estimated that over 300,000 people have been buried in the cemetery. The first recorded was that of Mr John Alexander Burnett. Mr Burnett a merchant of the city associated with the company Dalgety Gore & Co and the then Secretary of the Melbourne Chamber of Commerce had died suddenly at his home in St Kilda on Wednesday the 25th May 1853 at the age of 36. He was interred the following Saturday. The first female burial was Jane Bell who died at the age of 20 at Brunswick on 9th June 1853.

As can be imagined those interred represent Melbourne's society from Colonial times to the present day. Prime Ministers, Premiers, war heroes, artists, sportspersons, philanthropists, explorers and other notables are all represented.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: A religious complex of five buildings. The Anglican Church has been present on this site since 1853. The oldest building is St Mary's Church which is a bluestone building designed by Lloyd Tayler and built by Pepper & Paton. It was opened on Sunday 10th March 1860 and, as reported by the Argus of 14th March 1860, at a cost of 2,987 pounds, 11 shillings and sixpence. The Church Hall, a single storey brick building, was built in 1914. The manse, a single storey brick residence designed in the California Bungalow style, was built in 1917. At 171 Howard Street there is a double storey clinker brick apartment building with four flats designed in the English Domestic Revival style and built in 1937. To the rear of the hall is a single storey brick kindergarten.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

The new century brought with it new materials and sustainable projects that depending on your point of view, are astonishing or an eye sore; they are designed to be noticed.

properties.PropertyDescription: Formerly known as the Cobden Buildings. A three storey rendered bluestone and brick retail and office building. Built for James and Robert Jackson in the Italianate Renaissance style by Taylor & Duguid in 1872. Sited opposite of what was Queens Wharf it was built for use as offices to cater for the mercantile trade. Some of the earliest tenants (1875) included the shipping agent Pierre Cornillon, M H England tea broker, commission agent Robert Johnston, accountant and land agent W F A Rucker, Binda & Co merchants and importers, financial agent James Gill, Massey White & Co intercolonial agents, Gipps Land Navigation Company and Edward Curr the Chief Inspector of Sheep. In 1955 it was purchased by the clothing company Fletcher Jones for 130,000 pounds and refurbished. The company utilised the building up until 2012. A legacy of this occupation can be seen in the two stylised trousered men relief on the upper facade.

properties.PropertyDescription: A ten storey concrete apartment building with ground level parking, retail and level one offices. Designed by Nonda Katsilidis and built and subdivided into three commercial and fifty nine residential units in 1994."One of the first new apartment blocks to be constructed in central Melbourne in the early 1990s, it promoted the benefits of medium/high density city living, sparked a regeneration of its immediate locale adjacent to the Queen Victoria Market and provided a successful residential model for the city’s redevelopment policies.Katsalidis’s design invokes exuberant decorative and formal effects to enrich the urban facade, using copper-etched vertical slabs, weathered copper cladding, mannered window surrounds, glass blocks, brutalist and expressive concrete forms often with serrated edges, and a highly articulated roof line.Internally the large building bulk is divided into four discrete sections and each given a unique name, Equus, Mondo, Roma and Fortuna. This has the benefit of creating a more intimate experience for its inhabitants and also reduces the scale of the building’s management and overheads. Peter Corlett’s bold sculptures announce each of the building’s entrances and highlight its baroque and playful qualities." (Australian Institute of Architects - Nationally Significant 20th Century Architecture).

properties.PropertyDescription: A three storey brick and stone former residence. Built by B Austin in two stages. From 1848-1852 the first two levels to a design by the architect Charles Laing in the Georgian Regency style. In 1858 an additional storey was added with the architect being David Ross. properties.VHR: The former residence at 300 Queen Street was designed in 1848 and built between 1849 and 1852 as a residence for J T Smith. Smith was a publican, theatrical entrepreneur and later Mayor of Melbourne. The architect was Charles Laing. 300 Queen Street is constructed of stuccoed brick on a bluestone base with quoined openings and a large fanlight over the main entrance. In 1858 a third storey and outbuildings were added to designs by architect David Ross. The building has a simple symmetrical form, hipped slate-clad roof, Georgian fenestration and austere detailing. 300 Queen Street was occupied by David Munro between 1879 and 1889. Munro was a successful railway contractor who later as a land speculator was bankrupted during the economic crash of the early 1890s.The former residence at 300 Queen Street is historically significant as one of the oldest surviving houses in the central city area. It is significant for its associations with J T Smith, one of the earliest settlers in Melbourne, and who subsequently was Mayor of Melbourne seven times during the 1850s and 1860s. 300 Queen Street is also significant for its associations with David Munro, one of the largest employers in the State as a successful railway contractor during the 1870s and 1880s.The former residence at 300 Queen Street is architecturally significant as an excellent example of the survival of Georgian styling into the late 1840s and early 1850s. 300 Queen Street is a rare surviving example of the simple but elegant Georgian form. It is significant as a design by two of Melbourne's earliest architects, Charles Laing and David Ross.

A four storey cement rendered Edwardian brick former warehouse and office building with a mezzanine. Built around 1903 for Sniders & Abrahams Pty Ltd cigar and cigarette manufacturers. The rear lane, Sniders Lane, is named after a principal of the company. The company's factory was located to the rear in Drewery Place. Their business was known for the quality of the brands of hand rolled cigars Escude and Aristocratica.  As a sales incentive the company popularised the insertion of cards inside the cigarette packs that featured cricketers, jockeys, football players and football club colours. These cards became quite a phenomenon and could be called the first 'craze' of the twentieth century. Some of the more upright members of the community thought of them as a social evil. They were attributed to an upsurge of gambling in the youth of the day and an increase in juvenile cigarette smoking. The children had invented a game akin to two-up by using the cards. Newspapers had reported on customers leaving tobacconists being pestered by children asking for the cards. Shops were burgled, cigarette cartons were rifled and the cards were stolen. A Mrs Robson from Carlton at the 1909 Australasian Women's Association annual conference said it seemed to be the national instinct of the colonial youth to bet on anything. She frequently saw large crowds of boys of all ages in the gardens gambling with these cards. The State Government was concerned with the upsurge in smoking by youths and in July of 1909 the Premier of the day, Mr Jack Murray, instigated a report on the matter.  By the early 1920's Sniders & Abrahams had left and the building was utilised by a succession of merchants up until the early 1960's when it was refurbished, converted to offices, named Insurance House and tenanted by Swann Insuarance Brokers. In 1984 it was occupied by Pacific Typewriters Pty Ltd and renamed Pacific House.

Divided into building properties namely QV Retail and Parking, QV1 and two being residential, MCC Creche (Pod H) and two office buildings being QV3 the Sensis Building and the BHP Billiton Building. The retail component is spread over several basement levels, along the lanes, ground and some lower floors. Designed by John Wardle Architects and the BN Group. QV1 on the corner of Little Lonsdale and Russell Streets is a concrete and steel 44 storey residential building designed by John Wardle Architects. QV2 on the corner of Little Lonsdale and Swanston Streets is a concrete and steel 12 storey residential building designed by McBride Charles Ryan. QV3 on the corner of Swanston and Lonsdale Streets are two interlinked concrete office buildings of nine stories and designed by Denton Corker & Marshall. The BHP Billiton Centre on the corner of Lonsdale and Russell Streets is a concrete and steel 28 storey office building designed by Lucas Architects. The MCC Creche Building facing Russell Street is a six storey steel and brick building designed by Kerstin Thompson. There are two carparks one of which is a commercial carpark with multiple entrances and the private carpark servicing the residential buildings with a main entrance off Russell Street.

properties.PropertyDescription: A Church complex containing many buildings. The main religious buildings consists of Wesley Church and its associated Manse, Sunday School and Sexton's Cottage. These were all designed by Joseph Reed in the Gothic Revival style.The Church, built in 1858, is a single storey bluestone building and is thought to have the earliest spire built in Melbourne. The Manse and Sunday School, also bluestone, were built in 1859. The Sexton's Cottage a single storey brick building was built in 1914.The former Princess Mary Club at 118-122 Lonsdale Street was a four storey concrete building. It was originally built as a hostel for country girls. Designed by Alec S Eggleston in the Modern Tudor style it was built by JSG Wright in 1926. It originally incorporated a motorcar show room on the ground level with a garage to the rear. It was demolished in 2017.Nicholas Hall on the East side of the property is a stucco covered concrete building. Designed by Harry Norris in the Moderne style and built by Clement Langford in 1938.Wesley House a five storey concrete office building at 148 Lonsdale Street was built in 1970.There were two further utility buildings to the rear facing Little Lonsdale Street at 117 and 125-129. Both were single storey and brick and were built around 1915 and demolished in 2017.To open area to the rear, was used as an open air commercial carpark prior to development in 2017. Of note is a bronze statue of John Wesley by Paul Montford in the forecourt which was erected in 1936. There is an olive tree of State significance located in the former carpark. It was planted in 1875 by Mrs Mars Miller and is one of the oldest exotic trees in Victoria.The following is an extract from a Government media release.Minister for Planning Richard Wynne has approved a $200 million redevelopment of the Wesley Church site at 118-148 Lonsdale Street, Melbourne.The approved permit includes conditions to extend the building setbacks, reduce overshadowing over Cohen Place and increase the separation to the nearby Regency tower.The redevelopment also includes ground and lower level retail space, a new ground level park and two public walkways through the site.The 34 level commercial office tower will sit on the eastern portion of the Wesley Church site with frontages to Lonsdale Street, Little Lonsdale Street and Jones Lane.The entire site is listed on the Victorian Heritage Register and the Heritage Council has already granted the necessary demolition permit for some of the buildings on site, including the Princess Mary Club.The office tower is part of a broader proposal to restore heritage elements of the site, including the Wesley Church, the Manse and the school house.The church has been unable to maintain its buildings and the redevelopment will fund the restoration and maintenance of the other buildings.The Uniting Church will be provided with space in the new office tower, providing a permanent home for the church and Wesley Mission Victoria.Recognising the historic significance of the Princess Mary Club, a plaque will be installed on site to mark its role in Melbourne’s past.Quotes attributable to Minister for Planning Richard Wynne“This new tower for the Wesley Church site will deliver more office space to the inner city without overwhelming the historic neighbouring church…..This approval allows the Wesley Church to continue with its plan to fund the Wesley Mission and upgrade the other historic buildings on the site”.

Red brick and terracotta tiles marked a significant shift in taste towards a more original Australian style from 1890 to 1920.
There are many other different Federation styles including Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and the popular Federation bungalow in residential areas.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: A four storey rendered brick former warehouse. Designed by John DeLacy Evans in the Queen Anne Revival style and built by Thomas Sanders for the jewellers Jacob and Benjamin Marks in 1889. The first tenants were the china, glass and earthernware importer Alfred Fullagar and the furniture retailers McKell Speedie and Co.. In 1970 it was purchased by the Commonwealth and refurbished and converted to an office building for the City Telephone Installation Centre. Refurbished, subdivided and converted to residential units on upper levels with ground level parking and retail in 1994.
6 storey rendered brick building. Built 1923  refurbished 1988.

The former Money Order Office and Savings Bank. A six storey rendered brick office building with ground level retail. Designed by Peter Kerr of the Public Works Office in the Free Classical style to harmonise with the nearby General Post Office. It was built by James H Sutherland in 1890.

Designed to be virtually fire proof it was severely damaged on the evening of 31 November 1907 when a conflagration destroyed several adjoining warehouses and shops. It remained in use as a telegraph office until the early 1980's.

The upper floors were refurbished and subdivided into residential units in 1999 and are currently being used as serviced apartments.

World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.

properties.PropertyDescription: A five storey cement rendered brick former warehouse. What was one of a pair of warehouses (the other was at 384-390) built for George Robertson & Company Pty Ltd. This company was Melbourne's foremost book selling, publishing and stationery manufacturer. Mr Robertson, from Glasgow, commenced business in 1852 with a shop at 84 Russell Street. Authors associated with the company included Adam Lindsay Gordon, Henry Kendall, Marcus Clarke and Rolf Boldrewood. Built on a base of Malmsbury bluestone it was designed by Twentyman & Askew in the Italian Renaissance style and completed in 1883. The first tenant was the ironmonger Briscoe & Co. It was purchased by the glazing firm EL Yencken Pty Ltd in 1904 and they held the building until 1957 when it was sold for £95,000 to the furnishing company Kornblums Pty Ltd. In 1964 it was purchased for £177,500 by the publishing company John Fairfax Pty Ltd who refurbished and converted it to an office building at a cost of £63,000.  Refurbished, converted and subdivided into 31 residential and one ground level retail unit in 1995.

A nine storey brick office building built for EL Yencken & Co Pty Ltd in 1939. The architect for the project was Cedric H Ballantyne and the engineer in charge was Clive Steel. The total cost of the project was 30,500 pouns. Refurbished with the addition of the top storey, subdivided and converted to 36 residential apartments and two ground level retail units in 1994.

A three storey brick building. Built for the locksmiths and agricultural brand manufacturers William Willis & Co as a showroom and offices in 1905. For some years after 1916 the upper floor was utilised by the Wayfarers Club who held fortnightly meetings there. This organisation was established to provide a place of interaction for working girls and women living away from home. The membership fee was sixpence. Refurbished in 1924 after being purchased by the Law Institute of Victoria with the creation of three shops on the ground and new offices on the upper floors. The building works cost 3,000 pounds plus 750 pounds for the new shop and upper floor windows. It became known as Law Institute House. In 1966 it was refurbished again combining two shops into an office fronting Little Collins Street. In 1990 this was converted back to a shop.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Interwar period continued the success of the California bungalow in the suburbs along with new varieties of Art Deco architecture, including Moderne, Streamlined Moderne and Skyscraper Gothic.
The ownership of cars brought with it the necessity for driveways, carparks and garages and so houses were set back.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
Federation brought the title of “Nations capital” to Melbourne between 1901 and 1927 and with it suitable grand styles like Baroque, Art Nouveau and Romanesque.
Red brick and terracotta tiles marked a significant shift in taste towards a more original Australian style from 1890 to 1920.
There are many other different Federation styles including Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and the popular Federation bungalow in residential areas.

properties.PropertyDescription: Formerly the Leitrim Hotel. A three storey rendered brick building. Designed by Henry Tolhurst in the Renaissance Revival style and built by Jason Fraser in 1888. properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The new century brought with it new materials and sustainable projects that depending on your point of view, are astonishing or an eye sore; they are designed to be noticed.
Museums, residential skyscrapers, stadiums and public and University buildings alike have been designed and modelled on computers in 3D and constructed with precision.
No one single style is dominant, with architects experimenting with highly conceptual and expressive styling resembling art and sculpture on a grand scale.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

properties.Display2: Argyle Square 153-159 Lygon Street CARLTON VIC 3053
properties.PropertyDescription: A public space. First surveyed with the plans laid out by Robert Hoddle in 1852. The Northern section originally contained a tennis court and the Carlton Bowling Club that was established in 1868. This closed in 1995. The Southern section's plantings and paths design was laid out in the mid 1870's. On the North Eastern corner of this section is a drinking fountain dedicated to William Ievers a businessman, philanthropist and City Councillor. In 2006 and in partnership with the Cities of Milan and Melbourne the Northern Section was redeveloped by the company 2Construct. This became known as the Piazza Italia and features new plantings and a central bronze solar clock surrounded by a paved area designed by Andrea Tomaselli made from porphyry stone imported from the Trento Region in Italy. Overlooking the piazza is a pavilion. On the Western Boundary is a bocce court.

World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
