properties.PropertyDescription: A former State Primary school site containing a two and three storey brick building designed by the Education Department's chief architect Henry Bastow in the Tudor Revival style and completed in 1885.Converted to the JH Boyd Domestic College in 1930. It became the JH Boyd Girls High School in 1979 and later part of the Victoria University of Technology and TAFE before being bought by the City of Melbourne for $10.5M in 2007.The original building was refurbished by the City of Melbourne and converted to the "Boyd" community hub in 2012.As part of the redevelopement a 1834 square metre parcel in the southern corner at 132 Kavanagh Street  was subdivided off and sold to the PDG Corporation and through a development agreement will transform the precinct and complete a vibrant community village. This development will consist of a mixed-use 110m building that includes residential and affordable housing, a boutique hotel, and retail and community facilities. The remainder of the site will feature a vibrant streetscape that links together key public spaces, including the new Boyd neighbourhood park. The park to be completed by the end of 2019 will create a new backyard for the thousands of residents living in apartments in Southbank.
properties.VHR: The JH Boyd Girls High School was constructed in 1884-1885 to the design of the Education Department's Chief Architect Henry Bastow. It opened as State School No 2686, replacing No. 222 St Luke's South Melbourne Church of England School in Clarendon Street, Emerald Hill. In 1929 it was amalgamated with the Eastern Road State School No. 1852. The building was reconstructed in 1930 by WH Bolger to become the South Melbourne Girls' School devoted to the training of girls in domestic arts. In 1932 it was renamed the JH Boyd Domestic College after its patron, a successful grazier, who bequeathed a large sum of money to establish a school of domestic science so "that women should be taught to manage a home correctly". The school occupies a prominent corner site on City Road, and is a two storey brick building with a third storey of one room and entry to a tower. It was closed as a school in 1985 after 100 years of operation. The extant section of the original school is a commanding Tudor Revival design executed in Hawthorn bricks, embellished with bands of cream brick and render mouldings. The Tudor influence is repeated in a castellated parapet and octagonal turret.The JH Boyd Girls High School is of architectural significance as one of the most ornamental and distinctive of the Education Department schools of the 19th century. It was the only 19th century State School to have a three storey central block, reflecting its prominent location in full view of the railway line from Port Melbourne to Flinders Street. The school's size and style are evidence of the rapid growth in population and wealth in Melbourne's suburbs as a result of post-gold rush consolidation and prosperity.The JH Boyd Girls High School is of historical significance as a reminder of earlier philosophies of educational provision, especially for girls. Domestic Arts schools developed in the years during and after WWI, at a time when there was a wider concerted push for 'scientific' mothering education. It was considered that mothering skills were not innate and needed to be taught, in the same way that domestic skills needed to be inculcated at school. The school's emphasis on the domestic arts demonstrates the different approach to girls' and boys' education that characterised the school system for much of the 19th and 20th centuries. Less emphasis was placed on academic achievement than on domestication, to produce young women who would find their place in private rather than public life. Nevertheless, these domestic arts schools were the predecessors of the Girls High Schools and, despite the emphasis on domestic skills, they were a means of expanding secondary education to girls at a time when State Governments were reluctant to provide post-primary education.Last updated on - October 6, 1999

properties.PropertyDescription: Single storey brick residence.

A property of four separate buildings.

Fronting Clarendon Street is Victoria House a three storey brick former apartment building. Designed in the Modern Tudor style by Phillip B Hudson it was built in 1914. Next door is an Edwardian single storey brick former residence now converted to a café. To Victoria Street is a pair of two storey residences named Clontarf and Clonmel. Designed in the Neo-Classical style by Gerald W Vanheers they were built for the dentist Richard Cox Thomas in 1909. He chose Clontarf as his residence.

The properties were consolidated in 1989 and subdivided into residential units in 1995.

properties.PropertyDescription: A five storey brick hospital with a basement. Built in 1937 with additions in 1958 and 1965. At 128-132 Grey Street the property incorporates a row of three two storey former residential terraces that were built in 1868.An old block of flats at 103 Albert Street and a hospital building at 124 Grey Street were demolished in 2018 and a new multi level hospital extension is currently under construction.
properties.VHR: 166 Clarendon StreetThe Freemasons Hospital was established by the United Grand Lodge of Victoria in 1937. It is the only known "intermediate" or "community" hospital constructed by a lodge or friendly society in Melbourne's inner suburbs in the early 1930s following the Victorian government's initiative to assist construction of hospitals to accommodate middle class fee-paying ("intermediate") patients. Inspired by modern American practice the new hospital, intended for use solely by Freemasons and their families, accommodated 60 patients and about forty nurses.The original five level reinforced concrete building, designed by architects Stephenson and Meldrum (later Stephenson and Turner) in the inter-war Functionalist style, was built by J R & E Seccull in 1936-37. The white cement rendered exterior was trimmed in Masonic blue, a pale shade on the balcony soffites and dark blue ceramic tiles highlighting the main entrance. A relief figure group representing the Freemason's crest and a geometric relief sculpture by Melbourne artist W L Bowles (1885-1954) is featured on walls of the lift motor room above the main entrance.The Freemasons clearly intended to extend the hospital or its facilities to adjacent land extending to Albert Street. In 1956-58 the hospital was substantially enlarged when the building was extended to a sympathetic design by architects Meldrum and Noad, making particular reference by its continuing balconies to the original. The extension has long been publicly regarded as integral part of the Freemason's Hospital.Further wings to the east were added in 1968 and 1977, and the front entrance was subsequently altered. Apart from respecting the scale of the original, these changes did not contribute to the cultural heritage significance of the hospital.The Freemasons Hospital is historically important as a major health institution established by Victorian Freemasons following an unprecedented boom in their membership after the First World War. It was built under the aegis of a 1929 Victorian government initiative to create private hospitals of sufficient size to offer treatment for both private and intermediate patients. Prior to this public hospitals catered only for the poor, and the affluent paid for their treatment in small private hospitals. The Freemasons Hospital reflects the increasing sophistication of medical treatments, surgical procedures and diagnostic equipment available by the 1930s which replaced home medical treatment for severe illness. Freemasonry, an oath-bound fraternity of men founded in London in 1717 to cultivate brotherhood and serve society, has played a significant and continuous role in the cultural life of Victoria since 1840.The Freemasons Hospital is a seminal example from Australia's great inter-war hospital building era, where hospitals became an identifiable building type of their own, and their design became the province of a number of specialist architecture firms. It is a significant early example of the work of Stephenson & Meldrum, later Stephenson & Turner, which became Australia's largest architectural practice. Commenced by Arthur George Stephenson (1890-1967) in the 1920s the firm specialised in hospital design. In 1954 Stephenson was knighted for services to architecture and became the first Australian to receive a Royal Institute of British Architects Gold Medal. He was awarded the Royal Australian Institute of Architects gold medal in 1964.The hospitals designed by Stephenson in the 1930s and 1940s, based on European modern movement principles, led the progress towards Australian functionalist modernism. Stephenson chose the modernist idiom for hospital design as it suited the advanced scientific, medical, and programmatic principles of the institution, and the functionalist expression allowed for simple planning and honesty of expression. The Freemasons Hospital was a seminal modernist building in Victoria, its severe horizontal balconies, contrasting vertical services tower and minimal decoration being radical for the time.The Freemason's Hospital also reflects the continuing architectural contribution to this building by Stephenson's original colleague Percy Meldrum, under whose later firm Meldrum and Noad the additionsof 1956-58 were organised. The 1950s wing, while deferring subtly to less elaborate tastes of that era, is a meaningful and considered extension to the earlier building and allows the entire hospital to present a united front to the Fitzroy Gardens opposite.128-132 Grey StreetThe Terrace at 128-132 Grey Street was built in 1868 for Thomas Russell, a produce merchant and auctioneer. The Terrace was designed by architects Crouch and Wilson.This two storey, three house Terrace is constructed of bichromatic brick. The body of the Terrace is in tuck-pointed brown brick, contrasting to the cream brick piers and cornice. At ground floor level, the Terraces comprise a recessed porch with arched entrance against the party walls and two windows with architrave mouldings. The upper storeys each comprise three windows with moulded cement architraves and hoods below a dentillated cornice and decorative parapet.Four large rendered brick piers and a wrought iron palisade fence separate the front gardens from the street.Substantial alterations were made at the rear of the Terrace in the early 1990s, and the original service wings were demolished. However at the front the original interior planning and circulation spaces are still clear and the main rooms are structurally mostly intact. The main facade has been restored to reveal the crisp tuck-pointed polychrome brickwork.The Terrace at 128-132 Grey Street is of architectural significance for demonstrating a transitional stage in the design and development of Terrace housing. It is an excellent example of the link between the earlier, simpler and more austere Terraces of the 1850s and the more decorated types of the 1870s and 1880s with their profusion of cast iron and classical detailing.The Terrace at 128-132 Grey Street is unusual as an early example of the use of bichromatic brickwork in a Terrace building. Architects Crouch and Wilson favoured the use of bichromatic brickwork in several of their church designs in this period.

properties.PropertyDescription: The residence of the anglican Archbishop of Melbourne since 1853. Known for its picturesque landscape and substantially intact gardens on a large block, Bishopscourt was first designed by Architects Newson and Blackburn in 1849. Construction began but was delayed by the onset of the Gold rush with labour shortages. In 1851 architects Russell and Thomas completed the building in 1853.When completed Bishopscourt consisted of a two storey bluestone building with Tower built in the Italianate style along with a single storey wing which was demolished and replaced with a brick wing in 1903. Bishopscourt became Government House temporarily between 1874 & 1876 and has been the subject of much renovation over the years as occupants changed.
properties.VHR: The elevated site for Bishopscourt was selected by BishopPerry, first Bishop of Melbourne, in 1848. Tenders for Bishopscourt were called by architects Newson and Blackburn in 1849. The site was partly cleared and construction began only to be delayed by labour shortages caused by the onset of the Gold Rush. In 1851 architects Russell andThomas called tenders for the completion of Bishopscourt, and by January 1853 it was ready for occupation by Bishop Perry and his wife. When completed in 1853 Bishopscourt consisted of a two-storey bluestone building with tower, flanked on the north side by a one-storey wing. In late 1854 architect Charles Swyer was engaged to lay out the grounds but it is unknown what these works actually were. It is possible that Newson and Blackburn were the principle garden designers, siting the residence in its corner position east of an ancient River Red Gum which survived on the site until the 1990s. In 1857 a reservation was made for a cathedral to be built alongside Bishopscourt, between Hotham and GeorgeStreets, but eventually the parish church of Holy Trinity used the site. Bishopscourt became Government House temporarily between 1874 and 1876. Fifty years after its construction Bishopscourt was found costly to maintain, inconvenient and unsatisfactory as a residence and a recommendation was made for its demolition and replacement. There was much deliberation and a compromise was met and in 1903 the north bluestone wing was demolished and replaced with a brick wing. Architects Inskip and Butler who also altered the gardens at this time designed the Federation Queen Anne Domestic style red brick wing. Later additions were carried out on the east side of the red brick section in the 1960s. Of the original 1853 house only the bluestone exterior and tower survive. The interior of the building has been altered many times as Bishopscourt was renovated before each new bishop or archbishop moved in.Bishopscourt is of historical and social significance as the oldest house in East Melbourne and as the residence of the Anglican Bishop and laterArchbishop of Melbourne since 1853. Being the last intact urban estate in the City of Melbourne the grounds of Bishopscourt are of outstanding historical significance. Bishopscourt is a rare surviving example within inner Melbourne of a mansion with its garden setting still remaining substantially intact. The Bishopscourt gardens are of social significance as they have been the venue of official hospitality, garden parties, fetes and carnivals over many years.Bishopscourt is of architectural significance as the bluestone section of the house is an important example of early Melbourne architecture. Its assymmetrical form with tower and arcades was the precursor of many grand Melbourne mansions. The rubbled bluestone, simple mouldings and French windows reflect early building techniques. The 1903 red brick addition is of architectural interest as an interesting solution to a design problem and for its detailing to enable its integration with the 1853 bluestone section. Bishopscourt is of great aesthetic significance for the relationship between the residence and grounds, forming an impressive space that continues the grand proportions of the adjacent Fitzroy Gardens. The position of the residence and the picturesque landscape with a sweeping drive and lawn creates the illusion of much larger grounds. The enclosed formal south garden with fountain is also of aesthetic importance contributing to the picturesque landscape.The Bishopscourt gardens have landscape and scientific significance for their collection of mature plants, particularly trees of evergreen and deciduous species. Because of their historic, aesthetic, botanical and in certain instances scientific (notably Ilex perado subsp. platyphylla and Ficus rubiginosa) significance, the trees recorded in the extent of registration provide an important contribution and context to the place. The north east corner of the site in particular is of archaeological importance for its potential to yield information on the outbuildings, cess pits and glasshouses which once occupied the site.

Named after Cardinal John Henry Newman the English writer and theologian. He was an Anglican clergyman and teacher at Oxford University. He became a Roman Catholic in 1845 and was integral in the establishment of the Catholic University of Ireland in 1854.
The land was granted to the Roman Catholic Church from the Crown in 1882. It wasn't until 1914 that under the leadership of Archbishop Thomas Carr a committee was formed to facilitate the erection and endowment of the college. It was decided to entrust the administration of the College to the Society of Jesus. In 1915 the Committee headed by the Coadjutor-Archbishop the Rev. Dr Daniel Mannix appointed the American architect Walter Burley Griffin and a local architect Augustus Fritsch to design the College. At the time Mr Griffin was the architect in charge of the design of the Federal Capital. Mr Fritsch was well known and used extensively by the Church in the design of ecclesiastical buildings. Mr Griffin in partnership with his wife Marion Mahony and brother-in-law Roy Alstan Lippincott submitted the plans and Mr Bart Moriaty a builder from Ballarat was contracted to build the College. On Pentecost Sunday, 11th June 1916 the Foundation Stone was laid by Archbishop Carr. This was a quiet and solemn affair. That evening at St Patrick's Cathedral, as reported by the Catholic Press Newspaper of 15th June 1916, at a meeting of the Committee and subscribers to the project Archbishop Mannix said that on that day the foundation stone had been blessed and laid in private, because his Grace Archbishop Carr was averse from public celebrations while the dreadful war was being waged. The College was completed in early 1918 and on Monday, March 4th the first students entered the College.  On Sunday, March 24th the blessing and formal opening were performed by the Apostolic Delegate Archbishop Bartolomeo Catteneo. Unlike the laying of the foundation stone this was quite a celebratory affair with over 35,000 people attending. As reported by the Argus newspaper on the following day a few small Sinn Fein flags were at times raised in the crowd. A feeling for the event was well conveyed by the newspaper when reporting on the speeches given by the dignitaries. Bishop Patrick Phelan of Sale humoured the assembled when on remarking on Archbishop Mannix's contribution said that the life of Dr Mannix was in great danger. (Laughter.) He was threatened with internment and transportation. (Laughter.) The danger, he said, was that Dr Mannix would be smothered with the affections of his people. (Cheers.) The State Police had failed to rescue him from that danger, and the Commonwealth Police should be tried. (Great laughter.) The Prime Minister (Mr Hughes) should wish to protect Dr Mannix more than anyone else in the Commonwealth. (Great laughter.) The Reverend Maurice Joseph O'Reilly, the rector of St. John's, College Sydney, considered it a dreadful thing that the democracy which so richly endowed our Universities should get no return for the money spent. During the referenda campaigns not a prominent man at the Sydney University took up the cause of liberty on behalf of the people. If the young men of Newman College were not going to be Australians first, and be true to the principals of Australian democracy, he would prefer that an earthquake should demolish the building. (Cheers.) Archbishop Mannix who was received with cheering dedicated part of his speech to the recently deceased Archbishop Carr saying that the college was the dream and ambition of the late Archbishop, and it was a monument to the magnificent work done by Dr Carr during 30 years in Melbourne. Of reinforced concrete construction dressed with Barabool sandstone the original building consists of two, two storey residential wings known as Mannix and Carr Wings radiating from a central domed refectory. The dome was originally clad with terracotta tiles but these were replaced with copper sheeting around 1935. Part of the dome was originally used as an infirmary. In 1919 when the pandemic influenza was wreaking havoc throughout Melbourne the first matron, Miss Ryan, was conspicuous in her tending and ministrations to the many that had succumbed to this illness. Dr Mannix in a report detailed in the first College magazine referring to the administration of the first 12 months said We feel that this success is due in a large degree to Miss Ryan whose practical ability and kindness have been felt throughout the College. Adding further to the efficient administration of the College he went on to say Newman College seems, like one of those more modern makes of motor cars, to be a self-starter.

Two further wings known as the Kenny and the Donovan Wings designed by Thomas Payne were completed in 1958 and 1961 respectively. The original furniture and fittings were designed by Marion Mahony specifically for the College and are still in evidence today. The landscaping was also designed by Mr Griffen and features many mature eucalyptus in particular Corymbia citiodora (Lemon Scented Gum) and Eucalyptus sideroxylon (Red Ironbark) being trees he was particularly fond of.
When built the College was unlike any architecture of its time and is thought to be the largest extant building designed by Walter Burley Griffin. The heritage architectural firm Eric Martin & Associates described Newman College as a new and vital amalgam of ancient, medieval, Oriental, American and modern elements, in the context of the Prairie School of Chicago. Originally without a separate chapel the contract for its design was awarded to W. P. Connolly in association with Payne & Dale. Designed in the Decorated Gothic style it was completed in 1942.
In 1978 a two storey residential apartment building of six units known as Murphy Court was completed.
The final building completed was the Academic Centre and is utilised by both Newman and St Mary's Colleges. Designed by Edmond & Corrigan in a Post-Modernist style it is constructed of pre-cast concrete and was completed in 2004.
properties.Architect: Walter Burley Griffin and Augustus Fritsch, Thomas Payne, W.P Connolly with Payne & Dale
properties.SignificantEvent: On Penracost Sunday 11th June 1916 the Foundation Stone was laid by Archbishop Carr.
properties.SignificantName: Newman College, Mannix and Carr Wings, Murphy Court
properties.PeriodLongDescription:
Federation brought the title of “Nations capital” to Melbourne between 1901 and 1927 and with it suitable grand styles like Baroque, Art Nouveau and Romanesque.
Red brick and terracotta tiles marked a significant shift in taste towards a more original Australian style from 1890 to 1920.
There are many other different Federation styles including Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and the popular Federation bungalow in residential areas.

properties.Display2: Queen's College 1-17 College Crescent PARKVILLE VIC 3052
properties.PropertyDescription:
A university residential college complex.

The land was granted to the Wesleyan Methodist Church by the Victorian Colonial Government in 1853. In 1879 a committee headed by the Reverend William Abraham Quick was formed in order to raise funds for the establishment of the college. In 1887 the first section of the main building was erected and Reverend Quick became the president. This building is a three storey sandstone building designed in the Neo Gothic style by Oakden, Addison & Kemp and built by Messrs Mullin, Bennie and Olivers. It provided for residential accomodation for 18 students with lecture rooms and a masters' residence. As it was opened in the Jubilee year of the reign of Queen Victoria it was named Queen's College. The laying of the memorial stone was held on 16 June 1887 and the honour of this was granted to Governor Henry Brougham Loch. During his address, as quoted by the Argus Newspaper, he was glad to hear that it was contemplated to extend the privileges of the college to ladies. He felt that he could only congratulate himself that he had not been called on to undergo a competitive examination with the other sex. (Laughter.) The day, indeed, be not far distant when there would be a lady in the position of head of Government of Victoria (more laughter.)….., but certainly, and to speak seriously, the characteristic liberality which existed among men would not prevent them from doing what they could to give every opportunity to come forward and compete in the strife.

Land from the original grant was donated and a female residential college which became known as St Hilda's was built in 1964.

Queen's College itself didn't become co-educational until 1973. The college quickly expanded and the Southern Wing built in the same style was completed in 1890 with further extensions in 1905 and 1910. An extension of the Northern Wing, known as the Tweddle Wing, was built to a design by Mr A Eggleston in 1923. Designed to compliment the original building it is constructed of Waurn Ponds sandstone. It features a central tower known as the Sugden Tower. The western four storey section completes the main building. The Raynor C Johnson Wing was built in two stages in 1961 and 1969 and the Parnaby Wing was completed in 1987. In 1930 the Nicholas Laboratories were built. This single storey rendered brick building with a two storey central tower was built from funds donated to the College by the businessmen and philanthropists Alfred and George Nicholas. It was originally utilised as laboratories for physics, chemistry and zooology. Later the building was refurbished and became the college's student centre. The dining hall known as Eakins Hall a single storey brick building designed by Bates Smart & McCutcheon was built in 1964. The single storey brick residential building known as Kernick House was built in 1975. Scott Terrace a single storey brick residence was built in 1998 and the Jack Clarke and Lapthorne buildings were built in 2000. The Graduate Residence a three and five storey brick building designed by John Wardle Architects was completed in 2012.
properties.Architect: Oakden, Addison & Kemp , Mr A Eggleston , Bates Smart & McCutcheon, John Wardle
properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.Display2: St Hilda's College 19-27 College Crescent PARKVILLE VIC 3052
properties.PropertyDescription: A university residential college complex. Established on land donated by the nearby Queen's College. Named after St Hilda who in 663AD founded the abbey and double monastery of monks and nuns at Whitby. This is thought to have been the first co-educational abbey in England. Opened by Sir Robert Menzies in 1964. Most of the buildings are two with some three and four storey residences. The most recent additions are the Brian James Wing completed in 2008 and the Academic Centre built in 2010. Originally established as an all female college in 1973 St Hilda's became the first residential college at the University of Melbourne to become co-educational.

properties.PropertyDescription: A residential college complex.The land was granted to the Presbyterian Church by the Victorian Colonial Government in 1853. The college is an eclectic mix of Victorian late Gothic and mid-20th Century Modernist building styles designed by some of the most eminent architects of their day. In 1877 a committee headed by Alexander Morrison, the head of Scotch College, was formed by the Presbyterian Church Assembly in order to facilitate the funding, design and governance of the College.In answer to the Church's appeal for funds the grazier and philanthropist Francis Ormond provided the majority of funds. So generous was Mr Ormond that at a committee meeting on 25 February 1881 a telegram received from him was read. It stated  I offer to bear the whole cost of the erection of that part of the College now completed, and I recommend that the additional sums raised for building be devoted to endowment and exhibitions. The foundation stone was laid in 1879 by Governor George Augustus Phipps the Marquess of Normanby who also opened the college in 1881. The initial enrolment of residents was twenty. Built by Robert Ekins of Carlton this original building is three storeys and faced with sandstone quarried from Barrabool and with dressings of limestone from Waurn Ponds and imported from Oamaru in New Zealand. Designed in the later Gothic style by Joseph Reed it features a 50m tower. The furniture for this building was custom made and was provided by the firm Messrs Moubray, Rowan and Hicks. Much of this remains today.Subsequent extensions designed by Reed & Barnes and Reed Smart & Tappin, companies associated with Joseph Reed, were completed in 1883, 1885 and 1889. In fact all structures designed in the 19th Century were associated with companies associated with Mr Reed. The Dining Hall completed in 1893 was built by Frederick Angel. Completing this main building complex was the chapel built to the rear of the tower in 1922.In 2012 under the direction of Lovell Chen Architects, and known as the Gables Project, a refurbishment creating two new levels inside the attic of the main building was completed.Wyselaskie Hall and House a two storey Theological Hall and residence designed in harmony with the main complex was built in 1887. It is named after John Dickson Wyselaskie a Western District grazier and benefactor to the Presbyterian Church. After his death in 1883 his estate had left a legacy of 10,000 pounds to enable the construction of this hall and 20,000 pounds for future payment of masters and scholarships.Allen House a two storey former Masters' Lodge was built in 1892 and is now a residence for graduates.MacLean House a two storey red brick residence designed in the Gothic Style was completed in 1929. It was named after the Reverend Hector MacLean who was appointed Professor of Old Testament Studies in 1927 and later became Moderator of the Presbyterian Church of Victoria.In the late 1950's and 1960's there was an expansion of building projects. Roy Grounds, Frederick Romberg and Robin Boyd three of Australia's foremost modernist architects were contracted to design these buildings. Attributed to Roy Grounds and completed in 1958 is the former Master's House. A single storey cream brick building it is now known as the Centre for Ethical Leadership. Also designed by Grounds is a single storey circular addition to Allen House. The Picken Buildings three interlinked three storey brick octagonal residences were designed by Frederick Romberg and completed in 1961.Built in 1965 the McFarland Library, now known as the Academic Centre, a two storey brick octagonal building was designed by Romberg and Boyd. This was substantially refurbished to a design by McGlashan Everist Architects in 2012. Another octagonal building known as McCaughey Court was also designed by Romberg and Boyd. This eight storey brick building was completed in 1968.In 2012 a refurbishment creating five residential rooms in the gable space was completed to a design by Everist Architects.The latest addition to the College is the Dalton McCaughey Library and Centre for Theology and Ministry. Built to the rear of Wyselaskie Hall it is a two storey concrete structure with copper detailing. Designed by Williams Boag Architects it houses learning facilities, a library and a chapel and was completed in 2007.
properties.Architect: Joseph Reed; Lovell Chen Architects; Roy Grounds, Frederick Romberg and Robin Boyd; McGlashan Everist Architects; Williams Boag Architects

properties.PropertyDescription:
A three storey brick residential college with a number of wings constructed in stages.

The College is named after Janet Marian Clarke the wife of Sir William John Clarke who was at one stage the largest landholder in Victoria. Mrs Clarke was a noted charity worker, benefactor and women's activist. With a donation of 5,000 pounds to Trinity College Mrs Clarke enabled the initiation of the planning and construction of the building. Thought to be the first women's college in Australia it was originally built as a female hostel for Trinity College in 1886. It became a hall of residence in 1921, an independent college in 1961 and co-educational in 1973.
The original central section built of red bricks with sandstone detailing was designed by Charles D'Ebro in the Tudor Gothic style and built by Thomas Corley. The northern wing known as the Manifold Wing was designed by Blackett Forster & Craig with construction completed in 1927. It was built for 4,000 pounds from funds after a bequest from the estate of William Thomson Manifold was gifted to Trinity College. Mr Manifold was a wealthy pastoralist who came from one of the original English families that settled the Western District. This bequest was qualified and in his will Mr Manifold stated that all students who entered this hall would pursue a course in domestic economy concurrently with studies for a University degree.

Some points from the speeches of some of the notable persons involved with the opening of the wing, as noted by the Argus Newspaper of 18 October 1927, give an interesting insight into the mores and attitudes of the day. John Manifold the son of William on referring to the qualification in his father's bequest said he feared that at first the students would regard the new course as something in the nature of an affliction. Nevertheless he hoped and believed that in the years to come the present students and those that follow them would feel grateful. Every home evolved around some woman and the happiness at home depended tremendously on her efficiency whether she did the household work herself or whether she had the supervision of others. Archbishop Lees in his address said that as president of the synod he felt almost ashamed to be present on such an occasion because it was not more than a week since its members had sternly and implacably refused to allow women who were still permitted to sit on the synod to take a share in governing by vestries. He could only plead that it was not his fault, but he was sure that the time would come when even those men who did not like a tingle of blue in a woman's stocking would allow them to sit on the vestries which they now fed, and help the Church which they now supported. The Governor, Lord Somers, who opened the wing, in his speech said he saw visions of the future when a woman's university course would combine knowledge of the arts and sciences with the knowledge of how to make life happy in spite of the arts and sciences.
In 1930 the southern section known as the Traill Wing designed by A & K Henderson was opened. It was named after Elsie Margaret Traill. Ms Traill was one of the earliest students enrolled at Janet Clarke Hall and was for many years a member of the Hall's committee. She was an active member of the Red Cross, Blind Society and Anglican Church. The construction of this wing resulted after a donation of 5,000 pounds by her. The wing was opened by Archbishop Head who, obviously concerned with the ongoing physical and mental fitness of the students, stressed in his speech that the students should Train your bodies in health and strength for ill health is a serious handicap in lifework. One often hears of nervous breakdowns in middle life due to overwork.
In 1974 a dining room extension designed by Mockridge Stable & Mitchell was completed.
In 1956 the Joske Wing linking the Manifold and the original central section was completed. This was named after Enid Joske a former student and later principal from 1928 to 1952.
The final section being an extension of the Manifold Wing was completed in 1964. This was designed in the Modernist style by Forsyth & Richardson. Known as the Scantlebury Wing it was named after Lilian Avis Scantlebury who was a former student, Red Cross leader, Trinity College Representative and in 1961 a member of the Janet Clarke Hall Inaugural Council.

properties.PropertyDescription: A residential college complex built on crown land vested to the Anglican Church in 1869. Trinity College is the oldest residential college associated with the University of Melbourne. In 1870 the foundation stone of the first building, the Provost's Lodge, was laid by Bishop Charles Perry and completed in 1872. This building of two storeys, now known as the Leeper Building, was designed by Leonard Terry in the Gothic Revival style and built by James Lawrence.During World War 2 it was utilised as a barracks and administrative centre for Royal Australian Air Force trainees. It is named after the Anglo-Irish academic and classical scholar Dr Alexander Leeper. Dr Leeper was appointed warden of Trinity College in 1876 and remained in this position for 42 years. Dr Leeper described his four passionate loyalties as the Church, the Classics, the Act of Union and the British Empire. It was through Dr Leeper's efforts that Janet Clarke Hall, the first residential college for women in Australia, was established. In 1878 the first purely residential building was completed. The three storey brown, red and black brick building with sandstone dressings featuring a four storey tower was designed by Frederick Wyatt in the Neo-Gothic manner. Known as the Bishops' Building it is named after Charles Perry and James Moorhouse the first two Anglican Bishops of Melbourne. The college was expanded further with the construction of the Clarke Wing. A two storey brick building designed by Edmund Blackett it features Romanesque columns and a cloister on the south side running the length of the structure. It is named after Sir William and Joseph Clarke, agriculturists and philanthropists, who had donated the funds for the erection of the building. Sir William was the husband of Janet Clarke of whom Janet Clarke Hall is named. During his speech on the opening of the building Sir William said that Victoria was his home, and he felt that the better its people were educated the happier they would be, and the pleasanter to live amongst.In 1880 the design of the gardens was laid out by William Guilfoyle. Still standing and in good order today is the College Oak planted by Bishop Moorhouse.  In 1917, as consequence of a gift of 10,000 pounds donated by the grazier John Horsfall, the Chapel was built. A red brick building designed by Alexander North and Louis Williams in the Decorated Gothic style it features styling in the Arts and Crafts manner. The impressive interior in particular has many decorative features which display this decorative styling with hard carved motifs featuring possum, platypus and Australian flora.In 1935 the four storey Behan Building was completed. A four storey residential building built of Barabool sandstone. Designed by Blackett & Foster in partnership with Anketell & K. Henderson it was built by Swanson Bros. of Little Collins Street. It was named after John Clifford Valentine Behan the second warden of the college and Victoria's first Rhodes Scholar.  The Memorial Building a three storey brick building was built in 1958 and opened by the Lieutenant-Governor Sir Edmund Herring in 1959. Designed in the Post-Modernist style by McGlashan & Everist it was built by John Holland Construction Engineers. The interior was completely refurbished in 2013 to a design by Peter Elliot architecture. Also designed by McGlashan & Everist is the Old Warden's Lodge. Built originally as a residence in 1960 it is a single storey cream brick rectangular building centred around a small court. Now used as the Theological School it was refurbished and extended in 2010. The new pavilion designed by Peter Elliott is a steel and brick structure linked to the original building with a glazed entry foyer.  Echoing the Behan building in style and standing beside is the Cowan Building. Completed in 1965 it is a four storey brick residential building. It is named after Ronald William Trafford Cowan the educationist and soldier who was warden of Trinity from 1946 until his untimely death in 1964.The library known as the Evan Burge Building was built in 1996. A two storey building designed by Bates Smart in the modernist style and constructed of split-face concrete blocks it features a vaulted roof. Named after Reverend Dr Evan Laurie Burge who was warden from 1974-1997.The latest major structure built is the Gourlay Building. Completed in 2007 it is essentially an extension of the Clarke Wing and interconnects with the Behan Building. Designed by Peter Elliott it is a three storey rendered concrete and brick residential building. Mr Gourlay was an ex resident student who became a successful businessman. The Gourlay family were very active philanthropists especially involved in causes related to education and health. In 2004 they endowed funds enabling the establishment of the Visiting Professorship of Ethics in Business.In 2012 at a cost of $5m the dining room linking the Leeper and Bishop buildings was refurbished with the addition of a new kitchen.
properties.VHR: The Clarke building, Trinity College consists of a long two storey structurewith stone dressings and a slate roof. It was erected in two stages to designsof Edmund Blackett in 1882-83 (architects: Blackett and son, contractor:RC Brown) and 1887 (architects: Blacket Bros, contractor: J Hollow) theconstruction of the first stage was supervised by W Pritchard. The building isnamed after its benefactors, Joseph and Sir William Clarke.This is a notable work of Edmund Blacket and his famous family of architectsand is their only contribution to the architecture of Melbourne. Thedistinctive aspect of the building is the fine proportioning of the facadesand the bay and elements with which they are composed, particularly on thenorth facade. The materials and details reflect the earlier building by Wyatt.The arcade of stilted segmental arches with irregular bays and unusual columnsis a notable feature.The building requires little restoration.

properties.PropertyDescription:
A residential college complex.

A brick building of three and four storeys with four wings enclosing a court. The East and South Wings were built in 1966 and the West and North Wings were completed in 1977.

Named after St Mary who as Mary Ward of Yorkshire in 1609 established a religious community at Saint-Omer and opened schools for girls. Under the direction of Archbishop Mannix St Mary's was originally established in 1917 as a women's hall of residence associated with Newman College.

Originally located at the former mansion 'Barbiston' at 148-156 The Avenue, Parkville the responsibilty for the admistration of the residence was given to the order of the Sisters of Loreto.

In 1966 St Mary's became an independent college and in 1977 became co-educational.

properties.PropertyDescription:
A University residential college complex.

Built on the site of the old Carlton Cricket Ground. In 1917 a committee was formed in order to facilitate the establishment of an independent non-denominational women's college for the University of Melbourne. Not until 1933 after much petitioning from the committee under the leadership of the president Mrs Lyndhurst Falkiner (Eilean Mary) Giblin and secretary Miss Elizabeth Lothian that the Crown Land was granted to establish the college. The foundation stone was laid by Lady Huntingfield on 17th September 1936 and by early 1937 the first wing of the college was completed at a cost of 12,418 pounds. Known as University Women's College nine students were enrolled for the 1937 academic year. The building was officially opened on Saturday 26th June 1937 by Lady Gowrie, wife of the Governor-General. The key for the opening was presented to Lady Gowrie by Kingsley Anketell Henderson principal architect of A & K Henderson the firm that designed the building. As a thank you Mrs Giblin presented the book 'A Room of One's Own' by Virginia Woolf to Lady Gowrie. The wing was named after Dr. Georgina Sweet the zoologist, academic and philanthropist. In 1920 Dr. Sweet was Melbourne University's first female associate-professor and for many years was president of the provisional council created to establish the college. Edna Walling the famed landscape designer donated her time to create the College's gardens.  In 1938 another floor was added to the building making it three storeys with a total 25 rooms. The southern wing of two storeys was completed and opened in 1939. It was named after Dr. Constance Ellis. Dr. Ellis was the first woman in Victoria to gain a Doctorate of Medicine.

Due to the constriants of the World War 2 the expansion of the College remained static until 1953 when the three storey cream brick Modernist style wing known as the Syme Wing was completed. The building was opened by Lady Brooks. During the speeches, as noted by the Argus newspaper of 5 March 1953, the principal, Miss Myra Roper said that the building had been designed to make it as attractive and feminine and as uninstitutional as possible. The paper reported that the bedrooms are single and individual and contain a bed, wardrobe, dressing table, bookcase and writing desk. They are big and airy and are painted in pastel colours.  The building was named after Eveline Winifred and Kathleen Alice Syme. The two were distant cousins. Eveline was a noted artist and former vice-president of the College's appeal committee. Kathleen was a journalist, former editor of the Age newspaper and well known for her welfare work. She was the president of the College's council from 1947 to 1954.
From 1953 up until the present time the college expanded considerably with wings and buildings opening in 1958, 1959, 1963, 1985, 1986, 1990, 1996, 1997, 2001 and the final phase of building in 2008 with the erection of the Recreation Centre.
In 1975 the College became co-residential and was renamed University College.
properties.Architect: Kingsley Anketell Henderson principal architect of A & K Henderson, Edna Walling the famed landscape designer
properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Interwar period continued the success of the California bungalow in the suburbs along with new varieties of Art Deco architecture, including Moderne, Streamlined Moderne and Skyscraper Gothic.
The ownership of cars brought with it the necessity for driveways, carparks and garages and so houses were set back.

properties.PropertyDescription: Office complex of five interlinked buildings incorporating several older buildings with basement parking and ground level retail. These include :61 Spring Street a two storey cement rendered brick former residence. Designed by Leonard Terry in The Renaissance Revival style and built in 1877. Noted for having been the Office of the Prime Minister from 1901-1912 and the office of the War Cabinet from 1914-1918.5-7 Collins Street a three storey rendered brick former residence. Designed by Lloyd Tayler in the Renaissance Revival style and built in 1884 by Martin & Peacock.9 Collins Street 'Grosvenor Chambers' a three storey rendered brick building. Designed by Oakden Addison & Kemp and built by JP Davison in 1887. Originally designed as a purpose built artists' studio it has over the years been the studio of the likes of Tom Roberts, Arthur Streeton, Clara Southern, Jane Sutherland, Charles Conder, E. Phillips Fox, John Longstaff, Max Meldrum, Mirka Mora, Albert Tucker and Wolfgang Sievers. Twin concrete office towers of seven and eighteen storeys designed by Denton Corker Marshall and Robert Peck Von Hartel Trethowan and built in 1984. An overhead walkway joins with 12-20 Flinders Lane.
properties.VHR: The former residence on the south west corner of Collins and Spring Street was built for a wealth pastoralist, William Campbell (1810-96) in 1877 to a design by architect Leonard Terry. The house, of cement rendered brick construction, originally extended south along Spring Street, but the four storey service wing was demolished in 1975. The surviving two storey section contains the principal rooms. After Campbell permanently left Victoria in 1882 the house was let for a while to William McCulloch (1832-1909). McCulloch was Member of the Legislative Council for Eastern (Gippsland) Province between 1880 and 1903. Later the house was let to members of the pastoralist Chirnside family. Between 1887 and 1901 61 Spring Street was owned by eye and ear surgeons.In 1901 the newly formed Commonwealth of Australia purchased the house, conveniently located close to parliament, for use as ministerial and departmental offices. The office of the Prime Minister was located in the building from 1901 until 1912, when it was relocated to a new purpose-built Commonwealth office block in Treasury Place. Between 1901and 1912 eight prime ministers occupied the 61 Spring Street - Barton, Deakin (three times), Watson, Reid and Fisher (twice). The Commonwealth continued to use the building until the late 1920s when all departments were transferred to the new national capital in Canberra.Internally the house retains its original plan and circulation spaces, including the large entrance hall and the main stair with cast iron balustrades. The large stairwell window is in the form of a Palladian motif, with a large central window flanked by two smaller, narrower panes. The central pane of glass is etched with the Campbell crest, a repeating Scottish thistle motif, and the date 1877.The former residence at 61 Spring Street is architecturally significant as a rare example of a substantial and largely intact nineteenth century townhouse surviving in the central business district. It has few peers as a townhouse. For its high level of integrity it may be compared to a much earlier house, 300 Queen Street, finished in c1858.The former residence at 61 Spring Street is architecturally significant as a distinctive town house example of Leonard Terry's work. Terry was a distinguished architect who produced a great number of notable buildings throughout Victoria, including many churches, banks and commercial buildings. 61 Spring Street draws on Terry's favoured Renaissance Revival idiom, which is clearly expressed in many of his banks and particularly at the nearby Melbourne Club finished in 1858. However, 61 Spring Street is a less rigorous working by Terry of the Renaissance Revival theme, particularly in the treatment of the projecting central bay with portico.The former residence at 61 Spring Street is historically and socially significant for its association with its original owner William Campbell, one of Australia's wealthy and prominent pastoralists, and with subsequent occupants including the noted Victorian businessman, pastoralist and politician William McCulloch, and members of the prominent Chirnside family. It is also historically and socially significant as the office of the Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of Australia, and other government ministries and departments when the seat of federal government was in Melbourne, prior to its transfer to Canberra in 1927.

The Rialto Towers are an iconic landmark of Melbourne's skyline. Consisting of twin towers of 66 and 38 storeys, a podium building and includes five basement levels of parking.Designed by Gerard de Preu & Partners and Perrot Lyon Mathieson Pty Ltd and built by the Grollo Group between 1982 and 1986. The original development included the restoration of the former Rialto and Winfield buildings as a hotel, and redevelopment of the York Butter Factory.Noted for its sheer glass/mirror curtain facade, the taller tower was the tallest office building in Australia up until 1991.Mid 1998 saw the completion of a new entrance plaza from Collins Street. This involved the refurbishment of the office towers foyer and the redevelopment of the plaza and lobby to give more natural light and greater protection from the weather.In 2015 a nineteenth century 3-level bluestone and rendered brick building was demolished to accommodate the Rialto Regeneration Project. The Rialto Regeneration project was completed in early 2017 and included the construction of the 6-storey Podium building located on the corner of Collins and King Streets at the base of the two existing towers.

A five storey reinforced concrete office building with basement parking and ground level retail. Designed by Stewart Calder in association with Reid & Pearson in the International style and built as offices and showrooms for McPherson's Proprietary Limited in 1935. McPherson's was a tool and machinery manufacturing company. The company was founded by Sir William McPherson a well respected industrialist, philanthropist and Nationalist politician who was Premier of Victoria from 1928 to 1929. It was owned and utilised by the company up until 1974 when it was sold to the Melbourne & Metropolitan Board of Works who refurbished it and converted it to a research facility containing the Board's chemical and microbiological laboratories. Refurbished and subdivided into ground level retail and a mix of residential and office units in 2004. An additional level was added in 2006 with the rooftop converted to a childcare facility. Recognised as a notable example of the International streamlined Moderne style. Of note are the broad bands of glass and terracotta faience and a band of black vitrolite running above the showroom windows.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

Federation brought the title of “Nations capital” to Melbourne between 1901 and 1927 and with it suitable grand styles like Baroque, Art Nouveau and Romanesque.

There are many other different Federation styles including Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and the popular Federation bungalow in residential areas.

The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: Known as the Lygon Buildings. A three and two storey row of rendered brick shops and residences. There were originally twelve shops fronting Lygon Street and three on Queensberry Street. Designed by George De Lacy Evans in the Free Classical style and built by Cockram & Co in 1888. It still features the original shop fronts. The original verandah had disappeared by the mid 1950's and was reinstated in the 1970's. Among the original tenants were Henry Evans Bootmaker, Mrs M King Milliner, Samuel Epstein Draper, Maria Murphy Dressmaker, W Lugg Estate Agent, R Price and Son Clothiers, Harris Bros Tailors, Miss Burke Costumiere, Mrs J R Johnstone Costumiere, Morris Eleman Hairdresser and Mr Prescott Confectioner.  Refurbished and sub-divided into fifteen commercial/retail units and thirty seven residential units in 1991. It is the largest and most intact Victorian era retail terrace in Melbourne.

properties.Display2: Kelvin Club 14-30 Melbourne Place MELBOURNE VIC 3000
properties.PropertyDescription: A two storey brick former warehouse and factory. Built by Edward Delbridge for the businessman and investor Mr John Boyd Watson in 1871. Mr Watson had made his fortune in the Bendigo gold fields, most notably as owner of the Kentish mine. This mine was to yield 13 tons of gold between 1871 to 1880. First utilised as a printery the first tenant was Stanford & Co. In 1927 it was refurbished and converted to a radio studio and in May the Broadcasting Co of Australia's station 3LO began broadcasting there. In the following year radio station 3AR began operating there in an adjoining studio. In 1939 it was in 3LO's studio that  Prime Minister Mr Bob Menzies broadcast Australia's declaration of war against Germany. In 1941 the radio stations had left and transferred their operations to Broadcast House at 458 Lonsdale Street. In 1944 the upper level was refurbished and converted to radio station 3AW's Radio Theatre and remained here until 1956. The Kelvin Club leased the ground floor in 1946 and in 1950 purchased the building for 25,000 pounds. After the departure of 3AW the Kelvin Club refurbished the building and became the sole occupier.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

An unusual apartment apartment complex of fourteen units consisting of a row of three Victorian terraces and a refurbished warehouse. The conversion was designed and developed by the Largga Partnership which was formed from the architectural firms Andrew Reed & Associates and Gunn & Hayball. The project was completed in 1979 and is thought to have been one of the first in Australia to recycle and convert a disused industrial building into a residential complex. Fronting Millswyn Street are the terraces. 114 Millswyn is a two storey brick residence designed by the noted firm Reed Henderson & Smart and built by John Eadie of Richmond in 1889. Mr Eadie a respected contractor, who had played football for Carlton and Melbourne, was noted for his work while contracted to the Public Works Department having built primary schools, post offices and railway stations. The building was built for Mutual Store Limited as a residence for the mananger of the warehouse and livery stable that was located to the rear in what is part of the present complex. Mr Richard O'Brien and his family were the first residents. Mutual Store Limited, estabished in 1872, built the first department store in Melbourne. Their flagship store can still be seen at 256 Flinders Street. 116-118 Millswyn is a pair of single storey brick residences. Designed by the firm of James Gall of 11 Swanston Street and built around 1892. The main building to the rear of the property is the former store and warehouse built for Mutual Store Limited in 1924. A four storey brick building with a basement it was built on the site of another store and livery stables that had been on the site since the late 1870's. A company related to the firm of Maples Furniture had purchased the site in 1963. By the mid 1970's it was vacant. Refurbished and converted to six apartments the top two storeys each contain a single penthouse. A two storey former warehouse attached to the main building has been converted to two units with a mezzanine. A former garage built in the early 1930's has been converted to a single unit with a mezzanine. This was refurbished and extended in 2002. The property features a landscaped garden and a swimming pool.

The former Royal Institute for the Blind. A complex of several buildings built initially for The Victorian Asylum and School for the Blind. The original building, a three storey bluestone structure, was designed by Crouch & Wilson in the Gothic Revival style and built in 1868. Further extensions were added in 1872. Ormond Hall fronting Moubray Street is a three storey building with a four storey tower. Designed by Nathaniel Billing & Son it was built in 1891. It includes a front extension built in 1921. The property includes a three storey brick factory built in the late 1920's. In 2004-2005 the complex was refurbished and developed into a conference centre including a  restaurant.

properties.PropertyDescription: Originally known as ICI House. The first fully glazed wall skyscraper in Australia. A nineteen storey concrete office building with framed glazed walling and two basement levels of which one is for parking.Designed in the international style by Bates Smart & McCutcheon. The building contractor was E. A. Watts Pty Ltd and construction began in September 1956 and completed in 1958. The site was purchased in 1951 for £88,000 and the completed project cost £3 million.It was noted by the Age newspaper of 15th October 1958 that 'the project was a triumph for the architects and builder having completed in such a tight timeframe. More than 500 men were employed on the building at the one time. Elaborate safety precautions were taken and a full-time safety officer was employed, but despite this two workmen fell to their death'.It was opened on Thursday 11th December by the Chairman of Imperial Chemical Industries Sir Alexander Fleck. At 83.80m it was Australia's tallest building up until 1961. It features a landscaped garden designed by John Stevens and sculptor Gerald Lewers.
properties.VHR: ICI House on the corner of Albert and Nicholson streets East Melbourne, designed by Bates Smart McCutcheon. From its completion in November 1958 until 1961, ICI House was the tallest building in Australia. At 84m it broke the 40.2m Victorian height restriction by 43.6m and set a new precedent in height controls in the city of Melbourne. Its height, combined with its position on the eastern hill of the central business district, terminating the axis of Lonsdale Street, made the building a landmark.The building is an open plan concrete encased steel framed structure elevated on pilotis over what was originally an open undercroft. The main body of the building is clad with framed glazed curtain walling. The floors of the building are of precast concrete flat panels. The building is comprised of 19 stories, including the ground floor and two floors below ground. The service core is separated from the main glass clad body of the building and is clad in precast concrete panel curtain walling . While curtain walling had previously been used to a small degree on facades in Melbourne, its use on ICI House was especially important in that the whole main body of the building is clad with it.The building's main entry is now off Albert Street through a foyer that was sympathetically remodelled in 1989 by the original architects. This originally was the secondary entrance whereas the main entrance was through the landscaped garden entered off Nicholson St. The garden, its water feature and fountain, all of which remain intact, were the result of a collaboration between the architects, landscape architect John Stevens and sculptor Gerald Lewers whose fountain sculpture is an intrinsic feature of the garden. The provision of the garden assisted with the breaking of the height limit.ICI House is of architectural significance due to its considerable advancements in local construction techniques. These include the framed glazed curtain walls and innovative use of concrete, including precast reinforced units in structural members and flooring. The division of the glazed office space from the solidly clad service tower predates similar developments overseas.ICI House was a major architectural statement which contributed to Melbourne's position as a participant in innovative world architecture in the 1950s. Its design follows continued developments in international style modernism and draws its influence from buildings such as The Ministry of Education and Health, Rio De Janeiro by Niemeyer and Costa, 1937-43; Lever House, New York by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, 1952 and The United Nations Secretariat, New York by Wallace Harrison, 1953.ICI House is also of architectural significance as it was a landmark in the planning of the city of Melbourne. The building was more than double the previous height restriction enforced in Victoria and the design was permitted under the uniform building regulations because the site coverage was examined as a percentage of the total site area. This led to plot ratio determinations for city sites and the eventual redefinition of the central Melbourne skyline.The garden (along with its component parts ie: the Lewers fountain and the water feature) is of significance due to its role in determining the plot ratio that allowed the breaking of the height limit as well as defining the original formal entry to the building.

properties.PeriodLongDescription:
World War 2 brought to an end the Art Deco style and the rise of more functional and contemporary unadorned styles of modernism and the International style.
Modern architecture during the 1950’s was characterised by two main building types; the curtain wall office block (ICI House) and the radical, flat roofed glass walled house. The hosting of the Olympic Games in 1956 too, brought a hive of building activity and civic pride in an emerging International city.

The Victorian period can be classified by the discovery of Gold in 1851 which brought ballooning population growth and tremendous wealth. Renaissance Revival styles including Academic Classical, Mannerist, Italianate, Gothic and Filigree (decorative lacework) flourished. Architects such as Joseph Reed and J J Clark had a profound influence on the City at the time.
By the 1880s “Marvellous Melbourne” was booming with fashionable coffee palaces and rampant property speculation. Melbourne hosted its first International exposition. “Boom styles” borrowed from a variety of styles to create richly textured and complex buildings driven by wealth.
Deep recession followed with the land boom bust of 1893 and it was not until the birth of Australia with Federation in 1901 that significant building activity recommenced.

properties.PropertyDescription: Citation from Victorian Heritage RegisterChandos is a single-storeyed rendered brick house designed by the architect Nahum Barnet in 1885. It has a central, pedimented and parapeted entrance porch, an iron front verandah and a dominating balustraded parapet decorated with orbs. The main facade windows are grouped in two lots of three with a common bracketed sill. The front door has a transom and side lights. The hipped main roof is covered with slate and the verandah is covered with iron. The verandah flooring is tiled. The chimneys are corbelled. Internally the building is not elaborately finished but includes cornices, ceiling roses and marble fireplaces. The house's external decoration reflects classical elements as applied to many Melbourne residences during the boom period to the early 1890s.Chandos is of architectural significance as an excellent example of a classical villa design by noted Melbourne architect Nahum Barnet, a prominent architect in the four decades after the 1890s depression. Chandos is significant as an early example of Barnet's domestic work, and was perhaps his first domestic commission. Chandos is an unusually restrained example of boom style architecture, with distinctly conservative Palladian-style origins.

properties.PropertyDescription: In 1955 the Baptist Union decided to establish Whitley College as a centenary project of the Union and the foundation stone was laid in the centenary year 1962. The college was opened on 27th February 1965 by the Prime Minister, the Rt Hon. Sir Robert Menzies, KT.It was named after Dr William T. Whitley who established the first Baptist Theological College in Australia in 1891.From 1965-2017 Whitley College served as one of the twelve residential colleges of the University of Melbourne until the site was sold to a British student apartment operator (GSA).Originally designed by Mockridge Stahle & Mitchell in a "donut" shape, the building was also affectionately known as the "Drum".Undergoing a complete reconstuction in 2018, the new accommodation will accomodate 367 beds, nearly triple the original 130 beds. Two new floors will be constructed on the top of the rear of the Drum and a terrace at the front that will overlook Princes Park. At the rear of the site a new six-level building is being constructed.

properties.PropertyDescription: The Royal Exhibition Building is a three storey rendered brick building on a bluestone base topped with a dome. Designed by Joseph Reed & Barnes in the Free Classical style and built by David Mitchell between 1879-1880 for the cost of 70,257 pounds.The dome is based on the dome of the Duomo in Florence designed by Brunelleschi. The building was built for the Melbourne International Exhibition of 1880 and then used again for the Centennial International Exhibition of 1888. It was the site of the first opening of the Federal Parliament. For this purpose the interior was decorated by John Anderson and this was restored in 1994.The building was accepted and inscribed on the UNESCO Heritage List in 2004.Some notable features include:The Westgarth Drinking Fountain manufactured by Alexander McDonald & Co in 1888 and sited near the footpath in Nicholson Street.The French Fountain constructed in 1880 and erected in front of the Eastern nave.
properties.VHR: The Royal Exhibition Buildings and Carlton Gardens were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on 1 July 2004. The site was inscribed under Criterion (ii) of the Operational Guidelines for the UNESCO World Heritage Convention (1972) as follows:"The Royal Exhibition Building and the surrounding Carlton Gardens, as the main extant survivors of a Palace of Industry and its setting, together reflect the global influence of the international exhibition movement of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The movement showcased technological innovation and change, which helped promote a rapid increase in industrialisation and international trade through the exchange of knowledge and ideas."The Royal Exhibition Building was constructed in 1879-1880 to house the International Exhibition of 1880. It is the only major extant nineteenth century exhibition building in Australia and one of only a handful remaining world wide. It is set within the Carlton Gardens, one of Melbourne's finest public parks. The design by noted architect Joseph Reed was awarded first prize of £300 in an architectural competition. The successful tenderer was David Mitchell at a price of £70,257. Governor Sir George Bowen laid the foundation stone on 19 February 1879 and the main building was ready for the opening of the International Exhibition on 1 October 1880. Temporary annexes to house some of the exhibition were demolished after the exhibition closed on 30 April 1881. The subsequent 1888 Centennial International Exhibition was one of the largest events staged in Victoria's history. By the turn of the twentieth century the buildings and environs had become a combination of concert hall, museum, art gallery, aquarium and sports ground. The Royal Exhibition Building played an important role in Federation. On the 9 May 1901 the Duke of York presided over the opening of the first Federal Parliament, and from 1901 to 1927 the western annexe was used as a temporary State Parliament while the new Federal Parliament occupied the Victorian Houses of Parliament. In 1919 the buildings became an emergency hospital for influenza epidemic victims and during the Second World War were used mainly by the RAAF. From 1948 to 1961 part of the complex was used as a migrant reception centre. The Royal Exhibition Building was still widely used in the post-war era for popular exhibitions such as the Home Show. The building is cruciform in plan with the nave known as the Great Hall on the main east-west axis. The main dome is 60 metres high and sits over the crossing of the nave and transepts. The southern transept, which contains a 13 metre wide semi-circular fanlight and is flanked by two towers, forms the main entrance. The decorative scheme by John Anderson for the opening of Federal Parliament saw the dome was decorated in imitation of the sky and the pendentives adorned with murals. An unusual and interesting aspect was the decorated exposed roof trusses throughout the building. The decorative scheme, hidden under layers of paint, was recovered and restored in a major renovation in the 1990s. In 2001 the Royal Exhibition Building hosted centenary celebrations of the opening of the first Federal Parliament. On 1 July 2004 the Royal Exhibition Building was inscribed on the World Heritage List.Superintendent Charles La Trobe first planned the 26 hectare site of the Carlton Gardens in 1839 as part of the green belt encircling Melbourne which included Batman Hill, Flagstaff Gardens, Fitzroy Gardens, Treasury Gardens and the Domain. The original layout of the gardens was by Edward La Trobe Bateman and dates to 1856. Further redesign and planting took place under the direction of the State's leading landscape designers and horticulturists, including Clement Hodgkinson, William Sangster, Nicholas Bickford, John Guilfoyle and architect Joseph Reed. Reed and Sangster, who was also a nurseryman, worked in conjunction to ensure a suitable setting for the building, planning gardens, paths, entrances and other features. As well as the Royal Exhibition Building and the 1891 Curator's Lodge, first lived in by John Guilfoyle, the gardens contain three important fountains: the Hochgurtel Fountain, designed for the 1880 Exhibition by Joseph Hochgurtel; the French Fountain; and the Westgarth Drinking Fountain. The original perimeter fence was removed in about 1928 leaving only a small remnant and all of the bluestone plinth. The Melbourne Museum, designed by architects Denton Corker Marshall and constructed in the gardens immediately to the north of the Royal Exhibition Building, opened in 2000.The Royal Exhibition Building is historically significant as the only major extant nineteenth century exhibition building in Australia. It is one of the few major nineteenth century exhibition buildings to survive worldwide. Together with the associated landscaped gardens, the building forms one of the major surviving nineteenth century exhibition precincts in the world. The building demonstrates the wealth and confidence of the colony of Victoria in the late 1870s. It has been the stage for highly significant and historic national events, including the Melbourne Exhibition of 1880, the Centennial Exhibition of 1888, the opening of the Federal Parliament in 1901 and as the venue for the Victorian State Parliament from 1901 until 1927. The decorative scheme by John Anderson for the opening of Parliament in 1901 is of historical and aesthetic significance and is among the finest public art works in Victoria.The Royal Exhibition Building is architecturally significant as one of the finest and largest nineteenth century buildings in Australia. The stylistic choice of Renaissance motifs and the modelling of the dome on that of Brunelleschi's Florence Cathedral is emblematic of the sense of confidence of the young colony of Victoria in 1880. The Royal Exhibition Building is architecturally significant as the largest design carried out by renowned Melbourne architectural firm Reed and Barnes, who were responsible for many of Melbourne's most prestigious public buildings, including the Melbourne Town Hall and the State Library.The Carlton Gardens, the setting for the Royal Exhibition Building, are aesthetically significant for their nineteenth century 'Gardenesque' style featuring specimen trees, parterre garden beds, in a symmetrical design with the use of axial views and foci. The landscape features outstanding tree avenues, rows and specimen trees on the lawns, a curator's lodge, two lakes with islands, shrubberies and elaborate annual bedding displays along the southern promenade. The nineteenth century path layout is enhanced by magnificent avenues of trees, including the grand avenue of 26 Plane trees which frames the Exhibition Building dome, Elms, Cedar, White Poplar, English Oak and an uncommon avenue of 35 Turkey Oaks. Carlton Gardens is notable for the creative achievement demonstrating skilful garden design, and a landscape character which features plantings of Pines, Cedar, Araucaria, Cypress, Gums, Figs, Pepper trees, Elms, Planes, Oaks, Poplars, Canary Island Date palms and Washington palms, that display contrasting colours and forms which enhances the Gardens, Royal Exhibition Building and the local urban area. Josef Hochgurtel's Exhibition Fountain of 1880 is the only known work of the artist in Australia and is historically significant as an expression of civic pride in Victoria's emerging international importance. Hochgurtel's fountain is the largest and most elaborate fountain in Australia, incorporating frolicking putti, fish-tailed Atlantes, goannas, platypus and ferns.
